Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how a Democrat-controlled Congress might impact U.S. foreign policy, the start of coalition-building talks in Israel, and Ukraine’s timeline for European Union accession.

Democrats took back control of the U.S. Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a dramatic rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. With Democratic candidates making big gains in historically deep red states, even top White House officials have recognized that Americans appear to be tired of the administration’s playbook and want significant change.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how a Democrat-controlled Congress might impact U.S. foreign policy, the start of coalition-building talks in Israel, and Ukraine’s timeline for European Union accession.

Democrats took back control of the U.S. Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections in a dramatic rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. With Democratic candidates making big gains in historically deep red states, even top White House officials have recognized that Americans appear to be tired of the administration’s playbook and want significant change.

“[E]veryone knows why we lost,” Vice President J.D. Vance wrote on X on Wednesday. “And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

According to Vance, many voters’ frustration centered on the Iran war. Since U.S. and Israeli forces first launched strikes on Iran in late February, fuel costs have skyrocketed to record highs, making inflation and pricing concerns the No. 1 issue for more than one-third of Americans, according to an Economist/YouGov poll published in September. The cost of living for the average U.S. household has grown by around $2,000 since the war began, according to economists at Moody’s Analytics. And dozens of U.S. products, from medical supplies to computers to condoms, have suffered strains to their supply chains.

On Election Day, Trump appeared to make a last-minute bid to convince voters that his Middle East policies are adaptable, abruptly announcing that Washington will cut off $4 billion in aid to Israel by the end of this year.

However, that did not seem to assuage voters. Kansas saw a Democrat win a Senate seat for the first time in nearly 100 years, with other big party flips occurring in Texas, Iowa, and North Carolina. Michigan elected the country’s first Muslim senator, Georgia elected the country’s first Black woman governor, and New Hampshire elected the country’s first openly gay man to serve as a senator. All of them are Democrats.

With the left now poised to hold a majority in the Senate and House of Representatives when the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, experts expect that Democrats will crack down on some of Trump’s most controversial policies. That could include challenges to sweeping tariffs, new limits to military spending for the Iran war, and investigations into alleged corruption within Trump’s inner circle. Pursuing the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could well be at the top of that list.

Other foreign-policy priorities for Democrats may include improving the U.S. relationship with NATO; providing greater support for Ukraine; reining in U.S. boat strikes in Latin America; and requiring greater regulation of Big Tech, artificial intelligence, and data centers.

Trump has flip-flopped in recent days between agreeing to work with Democrats and vowing to veto everything placed on his desk. House Democrats, meanwhile, have already outlined a 100-day agenda to bring down the cost of groceries, reverse cuts to healthcare programs, and launch investigations into some of Trump’s cabinet members.

“Lawyer up,” Rep. Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, said on Tuesday.

Many foreign leaders appeared optimistic that Democrats’ midterm mandate will “introduce a new era in world relations,” as South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store stressed that U.S. politics may now better align with European priorities, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez compared the results to last month’s left-wing victory in Brazil.

Still, analysts anticipate that the road ahead will not be easy for Democrats. “[N]o one should kid themselves that the next two years are going to be anything other than ugly, chaotic, and brutal,” FP’s Michael Hirsh wrote. “Looking ahead to 2028, many of those newly alienated former Trump voters will be up for grabs. The question is whether a badly divided Democratic Party will be in a position to draw them in.”

Coalition talks begin. Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday formally accepted last week’s parliamentary election results, paving the way for party consultations to begin. His announcement came after Israel’s election commission said that a thorough investigation found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results.” A separate Shin Bet investigation into alleged foreign interference is still ongoing.

Herzog’s decision deals a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to sow distrust in the results, which saw his hard-right bloc lose its majority in the Knesset. Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly touted unsubstantiated claims of Arab-led parties stealing the election, including by allegedly receiving aid from Qatar; Qatar has denied any involvement. Nonaligned Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in late October.

Now, Herzog will begin meeting with party leaders to determine who will be named prime minister-designate. Most individuals are expected to back either Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc. However, that will likely depend on who the Arab parties choose to support. Several of Eisenkot’s allies have balked at the idea of allying with Arab groups, yet Arab parties have largely ruled out joining any coalition that includes Netanyahu.

Not on target. The European Commission warned Ukraine on Wednesday that it needs to speed up its reform efforts if it wants to meet its European Union accession goal, which is to conclude membership negotiations by the end of 2028. “The Commission is committed to support this ambitious objective ​but considers that to meet it an acceleration of ⁠the pace of reforms is required,” the body wrote in a report seen by Reuters.

EU membership remains a core foreign-policy priority for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Kyiv has long argued that joining the bloc would give Ukraine greater long-term security against Russia; the EU granted Ukraine candidate status in June 2022, mere months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. However, on Wednesday, the bloc outlined only seven policy areas out of 35 in which Kyiv could conceivably finish reforms before its 2028 deadline expires.

According to the commission’s report, Ukraine must now focus on improving rule of law standards, delivering an action plan on national minorities, and tackling corruption. Several major scandals have undermined Kyiv’s reform efforts, including controversial cabinet reshuffles as well as evidence of politicians and other elites having received kickbacks from defense contractors.

“Act of treason.” Indonesia deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to the capital of Jakarta on Wednesday. Although military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Muhammad Nas insisted that the movements were “a normal occurrence,” their timing comes as local authorities are investigating an alleged illegal wiretapping operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto.

Earlier this week, Indonesian police detained three senior police generals suspected of intercepting communications, accessing electronic systems, and deleting electronic data between 2025 and 2026. The incident allegedly targeted Prabowo and dozens of other prominent figures, including journalists, activists, and business executives.

“Based on the progress of the investigation so far, there are signs and indications pointing toward an act of treason,” Yusril Ihza Mahendra, the Indonesian coordinating minister of law, human rights, immigration, and correctional institutions, said on Wednesday, adding that the operation could have been part of a broader effort to undermine the government.

Already, Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was appointed as the presidential chief of staff just last month, has been dismissed. Listyo was a known loyalist of former President Joko Widodo, who is Prabowo’s biggest rival and remains highly influential despite no longer serving in public office.

The dachshund has long been a favorite dog breed among the wealthy and famous, from Queen Victoria to Andy Warhol. Now, a German art museum is celebrating the sausage dog’s influence across the ages. On Saturday, the Kunsthalle Bremen unveiled “The Dachshund: An Icon Off the Leash,” an exhibit featuring paintings, photography, stuffed toys, and other works of art by fans of the four-legged hunting dog. The dachshund was “like a muse,” museum director Christoph Grunenberg said, pointing to the impact that it had on artists such as Pablo Picasso, David Hockney, and Thorsten Brinkmann.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said the American people deserve an investigation into the Department of Government Efficiency while leaving The Center for American Progress. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker are calling for an investigation into the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), previously led by Elon Musk, as talks have heated up among Democrats to launch a probe into the multibillionaire.

Democrats are calling for an investigation into the Department of Government Efficiency, previously led by Elon Musk. (Getty Images, File)

The tech CEO helped launch DOGE at the start of President Donald Trump's second term to root out waste and be more transparent about the federal government's spending.

DOGE's efforts included deferred resignations and buyouts of employees at federal agencies and contributed to a significant downsizing of the federal workforce, which was reduced by about 250,000 employees during 2025, according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

Africa Brief: U.N. Peacekeepers Are Leaving Western Sahara. What Does That Mean?

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: A United Nations deadlock ends the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, local elections take place in South Africa, and Moscow tries to project an illusion of a successful Russia-Africa Summit.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: A United Nations deadlock ends the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, local elections take place in South Africa, and Moscow tries to project an illusion of a successful Russia-Africa Summit.

A deadlock between the United States and Russia at the United Nations Security Council on Friday ended a 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in the disputed African territory of Western Sahara.

The U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to monitor a cease-fire after a 15-year armed conflict between Morocco, which claims sovereignty over the territory, and the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks Sahrawi independence. It was also tasked with organizing a referendum for Sahrawi self-determination.

The referendum has stalled for decades. Last month, a U.S. draft resolution for the Security Council sought to remove “referendum” from the mission’s name and make semi-autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty the sole basis for future political negotiations over Western Sahara. It would have also scaled back the peacekeeping force by April 2027.

Russia vetoed the plan, instead putting forth a rival proposal to grant the standard one-year extension without imposing terms that favored Morocco. That, in turn, was voted down by the United States. The mission’s mandate subsequently expired on Sunday.

Morocco annexed Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony, in 1975, displacing more than 100,000 people. An International Court of Justice ruling the same year found no historical basis for Morocco’s claim over the area. Rabat now controls around 80 percent of the territory, which boasts rich Atlantic fishing grounds and phosphate reserves.

Currently more than 160,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps hosted by Algeria. International aid groups have denounced the U.N. Security Council’s failure to renew the mission and find a solution to the severe humanitarian crisis caused by the political stalemate.

Traditionally, Western powers maintained a neutral position on Western Sahara’s status. But in 2020, during U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, Washington broke with precedent by recognizing Rabat’s sovereignty over the territory in exchange for Morocco reestablishing diplomatic relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, Russia’s stance has been largely driven by its close geopolitical and economic alliance with Algeria, which backs the Sahrawi liberation movement.

The U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, in which Democrats took control of both the House of Representatives and Senate, could eventually lead to a more nuanced stance from Washington on Western Sahara, especially since many Democrats have expressed support for the U.N.-led process. But any immediate reversal is unlikely.

Washington and Moscow have traded barbs in the wake of Friday’s deadlock. Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., said that Russia’s veto prevents “historic steps toward finally ending a 50-year conflict.” His Russian counterpart, Vassily Nebenzia, said the U.S. plan would have “set back the entire process of resolving the Western Sahara issue” by disregarding “a just, free and fair settlement based on the principle of self-determination.”

Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s U.N. representative, also warned that the U.S. resolution would “not only torpedo the foundations of the U.N. peace process but would also have set a very dangerous precedent that threatens broader regional and international peace and security.”

Some analysts have echoed these criticisms. “Eager for a quick diplomatic win,” wrote Hugh Lovatt, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, Washington has “closed the space for negotiations and risks creating regional instability.”

A small U.N. team is now supervising a phased withdrawal of U.N. peacekeepers and the return of military vehicles and other assets to troop-contributing nations, including Egypt, Ghana, and Pakistan.

Security observers fear that MINURSO’s departure could lead to renewed fighting in the territory. Amid a security vacuum, some analysts fear Morocco may be emboldened to send in troops in a bid to grab more territory.

Wednesday, Nov. 4: South Africa holds local government elections.

Friday, Nov. 6: Zambian Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane presents a delayed 2027 budget.

South African elections. Analysts are predicting that South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday will show growing political fragmentation. The country is already ruled by a coalition government after the African National Congress (ANC) lost its 30-year parliamentary majority in a historic general election in 2024.

A few days before the election, Trump announced that South Africa, the largest beneficiary of the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), would be removed from the duty-free trade agreement starting in January. But with less than 1 percent of South Africa’s total goods entering the U.S. market under AGOA, the decision will likely have little impact on the vote. Instead, domestic issues such as crime, corruption, and a lack of jobs are expected to be voters’ priority.

Voters will elect councils in all 257 municipalities, but a heavily indebted Johannesburg—the country’s biggest city—is the key battleground.

Johannesburg’s debt has spiraled in recent years, with consumer bills and other debt still owed to the city amounting to 72 billion rand (about $4.5 billion), with Johannesburg owing more than $1.5 billion to its immediate creditors. The city has struggled to collect trash and provide enough drinking water. By some estimates, nearly half of the city’s treated drinking water is lost to underground pipe leaks due to infrastructure neglect and commercial losses.

Currently, the white-led, pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) is leading the pack in Johannesburg, where its former federal chairperson, Helen Zille, is campaigning for mayor. (Zille was also mayor of Cape Town from 2006 to 2009.)

Yet no party is predicted to win an outright majority. Most polls suggest the DA will win less than 40 percent of the vote in Johannesburg, followed by the ANC and two far-left parties: the uMkhonto weSizwe Party and Economic Freedom Fighters. The DA refuses to work with the latter two, which means it will likely form a coalition with the ANC or other smaller parties.

Déjà vu in Moscow. Moscow made a series of high-profile announcements around last week’s Russia-Africa Summit, including those concerning the sale of fighter jets to Ethiopia, Sudan’s offering of investment opportunities, and Russia’s support in modernizing Eritrea’s ports. Yet while some analysts have concluded that these evince Moscow’s rapidly growing role in Africa, there is reason to be skeptical.

None of these plans are new. Instead, Russia has highlighted and repackaged long-standing agreements to project an illusion of a successful summit. For instance, the delivery of 12 Russian Sukhoi Su-35 fighter jets and the planned acquisition of four S-400 air defense batteries to Ethiopia stem from a prior agreement signed several years ago; they are not, as the Moscow Times described it, “the summit’s highest-profile deal.”

Meanwhile, proposals for Moscow to modernize Eritrea’s ports have been floated since 2018. And Sudan, in order to secure military backing, has offered strategic cooperation with Moscow since the country’s civil war began in 2023.

At the summit, Moscow also announced nuclear power plant deals with several African nations, including Ghana. Yet apart from Egypt’s $29 billion El Dabaa project, decade-old nuclear power agreements between Russia and African nations remain unplanned. Russia agreed to build a nuclear plant for Ghana in 2015, for example, though it never came to fruition.

Congo mining dispute. California-based KoBold Metals, a mining start-up backed by Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos, has asked the United States for help in seeking U.N. Security Council approval to use aerial surveillance technology to map the location of critical minerals in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The company accuses China of using a U.N. arms embargo—which blocks the supply of arms and related equipment to nongovernmental entities and individuals operating in Congo—to prevent it from using the technology, according to a Financial Times report. China has said the allegations are “inconsistent with the facts.”

Congo, the world’s largest exporter of cobalt, has faced decades of armed fighting over its mineral resources. Chinese companies currently control around 80 percent of the country’s cobalt output.

Sudan’s fragmented war. In Africa Is a Country, Doha Ali, who fled Sudan’s civil war, argues that framing the situation in the country simply as a “humanitarian crisis” flattens its complex history and obscures the foreign interventions and proxy dynamics, including European anti-migration policy, that established the conditions for endless warfare.

“Wars do not simply happen; they are built. Sometimes they are built through weapons. Sometimes through money. Sometimes through diplomatic agreements signed years before the first shot is fired,” Ali writes.

Ali’s article is part of the series We Are Here: Sudanese Girls and Youth Hold Their Ground in Resistance and Remembrance, a collection of stories by young Sudanese people documenting their lived experiences of war and displacement.

Egyptian media repression. On Oct. 27, an Egyptian court ordered the immediate closure of Mada Masr, one of the country’s last prominent independent news outlets, and fined its editor in chief, Lina Attalah, 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,450) for operating without a license. Attalah will soon face a criminal trial and possible imprisonment.

This forms part of a wider crackdown against independent news agencies in Egypt, which has detained or jailed more than 20 journalists. In New Lines Magazine, a Cairo-based journalist using the pseudonym Anne Mostafa details Egyptian authorities’ 13-year campaign against Mada Masr and what it means for the country.

Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. X: @nosmotg

#6076. Keisha Lance Bottoms set to become first Black woman governor in US

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

The contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

#6075. 4 of nation's largest cities now led by socialist mayors after Tuesday's election, affecting tens of millions

'The Big Money Show' panel analyzes the market rally after Democrats took control of Congress. The panel says the key election issues were based on affordability and immigration.

Two socialist mayors were elected in the United States on Tuesday in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. which means four of the top 20 largest cities in the country have socialist leaders.

Los Angeles Councilwoman Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass and will take office in December as mayor for the roughly 4 million residents of Los Angeles proper.

Also victorious on Tuesday was DSA member Janeese Lewis George, who coasted to victory to become mayor-elect of Washington, D.C., a city of roughly 700,000 residents.

The list of socialist mayors in the top 20 most populous U.S. cities stands at four, after George and Raman joined Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST SWEEPS INTO DC MAYOR'S OFFICE, SIGNALS OPENNESS TO WORKING WITH TRUMP

Former Biden White House aide Yemisi Egbewole predicted the Democratic Socialists of America would struggle to gain national influence ahead of the 2028 presidential election despite recent electoral victories. (2019 Getty Images)

In total, the four cities are home to roughly 14 million people. That figure does not include neighboring suburbs, which could still feel the effects of policies enacted within city limits through crime, real estate values and the broader business climate.

Problems in a city can spill over into surrounding communities, while suburban residents who work in the city may also be directly affected.

Counting the population in the metro areas of those four cities, roughly 44 million people could be affected either positively or negatively by the socialist policies enacted by the four mayors.

DSA LEADER DISMISSES $49T COST ESTIMATE FOR SOCIALIST POLICIES AS A 'MADE-UP NUMBER'

Los Angeles Councilwoman Nithya Raman drew online mockery after touting a recent 'win' in her role representing her constituents. (Getty Images)

"This makes LA the fourth large city that will now have a socialist mayor, joining New York; Washington, D.C.; and Seattle," Heritage Foundation fellow Mike Gonzalez posted on X Thursday.

"Chicago's mayor is a buffoon, but he doesn't identify as DSA. America used to be an impregnable fortress against Marxism, then Marxists took over universities."

The socialist victories were not limited to city halls. Voters also elected seven DSA-backed or affiliated candidates to the House: Claire Valdez, Brand Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York; Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Angela Gonzales-Torres of California.

Several other candidates associated with socialist policies also entered Congress or were re-elected Tuesday.

Family members and supporters of D.C. Ward 4 Council member Janeese Lewis George, a candidate for D.C. mayor, cheer as she addresses them at Prince Hall Masonic Temple, a polling location, in Washington, D.C., June 8, 2026. (The Washington Post via Getty Images)

A recent Fox News national poll indicated 32% of voters have a favorable view of socialism, with 64% seeing it in an unfavorable way. But the favorable rating matches an all-time high, first reached five years ago, since Fox News first began asking the question in 2019.

And a September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans had a positive image of socialism, the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010.

The Fox News poll found that 51% of voters had a favorable view of capitalism, compared with 32% who viewed socialism favorably. Another 46% had an unfavorable view of capitalism.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

#6072. Andrews defeats Graham in South Carolina Senate shocker

Dr. Annie Andrews will be the first Democratic senator from South Carolina since 1998, according to AP projections. In a stunning upset, she defeated the incumbent Republican Darline Graham, who was hand-picked by Donald Trump to succeed her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, following his death in July.

A pediatrician, Andrews positioned herself as an antidote to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA agenda. Her campaign launch video hinged on measles outbreaks and the harm of anti-vax sentiments at the highest levels of public health. She described Kennedy as the “brain worm guy” and slammed Trump’s Cabinet as uniquely unsuited to their positions.

The race was never supposed to be close. South Carolina is about as red as you can imagine. The haven of cheap gas and fireworks hasn’t elected any Democrat to statewide office since 2006. Trump carried the state by 17 points in 2024.

Unlike her sibling, who shifted from staunch Trump critic to late-in-life ally, Graham was joined at the hip to the Trump administration from the outset. The president’s high disapproval ratings worked to turn the typical GOP lay-up into a closely contested race.

But Graham, a novice politician, did herself no favors. She flubbed softball questions around foreign affairs on the debate stage, a strong suit of her hawkish brother. Her dismal poll numbers pushed Trump to rally for Graham repeatedly in the state, cementing even stronger associations between the Republican nominee and Trump’s unpopular policies.

High early turnout among Black voters in the state also spelled trouble for Graham. The community, which is largely Democratic, turned out in high relative numbers and helped swing the race toward Andrews.

The Democratic candidate worked to avoid the associations with national party leaders that hamstrung Graham, refraining from appearances with prominent Democrats in the race’s final weeks. Andrews painted herself as a pragmatist, willing to work with national Republicans to score wins for South Carolinians. Late last month, Andrews received a shocking bipartisan endorsement from two former governors of South Carolina. Republican David Beasley joined Democrat Jim Hodges to support Andrews over Trump-backed Graham, saying Andrews was the only candidate focused on “making things better.”

#6071. American war hero details dire living conditions US troops face as Hegseth taps him to 'fix' it

Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer details troops living with mold, no hot water and broken AC as he takes on Hegseth’s push to fix military housing.

Some troops have gone a year without hot water. Others are sleeping in their cars to escape barracks without air conditioning. And some are asking for little more than drywall, spackle and paint so they can make repairs themselves.

Those are among the conditions Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer says he has encountered while touring military installations on a mission from War Secretary Pete Hegseth: Fix a barracks system plagued by decades of neglect.

"I would tell you that there's only a couple that I've seen that are good," Meyer told Fox News Digital in an interview Thursday.

DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL

Meyer, who serves as a senior advisor to the Pentagon's Barracks Task Force, has visited more than eight installations across the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps since taking on the assignment and plans to visit 30 before the end of the year.

"What I thought was gonna be a professional job very quickly turned into personal," Meyer said.

Extensive apparent mold and water damage cover walls and a closet inside military barracks inspected as part of the Pentagon's barracks overhaul. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

Medal of Honor recipient Sgt. Dakota Meyer listens to remarks during a reenlistment ceremony at the Pentagon April 17, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

At one installation, Meyer recalled asking a 19-year-old service member what she would change about her living conditions if she could "wave a magic wand."

"If she could just have a hot shower," Meyer recalled. "It's absolutely heartbreaking."

The Pentagon's barracks problems long predate Hegseth and have survived repeated attempts at reform.

A sweeping 2023 Government Accountability Office investigation documented serious health and safety hazards and found that the department lacked reliable information about the condition of its own barracks, could not determine how much of its facilities spending went toward them and provided insufficient oversight.

Congress and the military services have since committed billions toward improvements, including initiatives ranging from the Marine Corps' Barracks 2030 to a Navy overhaul of unaccompanied housing. Yet serious problems persist. As of this year, 12 of GAO's 31 recommendations remained outstanding.

Hegseth has sought to centralize the effort under a department-wide task force and accelerate improvements, and Meyer said the secretary has made clear that identifying problems is no longer enough.

"The secretary has made it clear to me he doesn't expect me to observe this, study it or to make it better. He expects me to fix it," Meyer said. "And that's exactly what we're going to do."

A damaged ceiling hangs over a bed in military barracks visited as part of the Pentagon's effort to assess living conditions for service members. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

Meyer, the only Medal of Honor hero to reenlist after receiving the award, said one of his first requests was for Hegseth to give the task force an "authoritative role," rather than simply create another layer of oversight.

The goal, he said, was to give the team the ability "to go out and make decisions, to be able to have impact, to be able to make change and to be able to direct where that funding goes and how fast it gets to our service members."

EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP

Meyer argued the problem is not simply a lack of money. Funding shortfalls, continuing resolutions and years of deferred maintenance have all contributed, he said, but so have layers of contracting rules and bureaucracy that can slow even relatively basic repairs.

A separate watchdog review found the Pentagon facing a $285 billion maintenance backlog across its broader military facilities' portfolio, underscoring the scale of the department's infrastructure challenges.

"When you look at the contracting aspect, it's easier for people to say no," Meyer said.

Funding is also part of the problem, according to Meyer, who pointed to Congress' failure to enact full-year defense appropriations for fiscal 2027. The Pentagon is operating under a continuing resolution through Dec. 11, which generally funds ongoing programs at prior-year rates while lawmakers negotiate a broader spending package.

"When you can't get a budget, when you're waiting on Congress to pass a budget, to be able to get the funding there, I mean, that is a huge issue," Meyer said.

A barracks room shows a sink without a basin and makeshift lighting installed around a bathroom ceiling during an inspection of service members' living conditions. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

But he also argued that the Pentagon has too often measured progress by how much money has been obligated or put under contract, rather than whether troops actually see improvements in their living conditions.

"Our service members don't, they don't live in our budget lines," Meyer said. "They live in the rooms that those budget lines are there to impact."

For Meyer, that has meant getting out of Washington and hearing directly from the troops living with the consequences.

"You can't fix these problems or understand these problems by standing on the carpet of the Pentagon," he said. "You've got to go out there and talk to these service members."

What he has heard, Meyer said, is striking partly because of how little troops are asking for.

"They're asking for a hot shower. They're asking for a place to wash their clothes. They're asking for a door that locks. They're asking to be able to go to sleep in a place that doesn't have mold. I mean, they're asking for light bulbs."

"They're willing to be part of the solution," he added.

Meyer stopped short of placing the blame solely on installation commanders, saying many want to improve conditions but have been constrained by a system that has normalized poor barracks for years.

"I think this is a multidimensional problem, and it's complex," he said. "I think that you have commanders out there that want to take care of their service members. I've seen that across the board. But ... they still have to have the ability to do that."

Meyer was far less forgiving of previous Pentagon leadership, arguing that years of investments and reform initiatives had failed to translate into adequate living conditions for troops.

"Don't kid yourself," Meyer said. "In the past ... it wasn't a priority to the leadership."

A window air conditioning unit and apparent mold and water damage are seen during inspections of military facilities as the Pentagon works to improve service members' living conditions. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

Previous administrations and military leaders did launch barracks improvement efforts and devoted billions of dollars to construction, renovation and maintenance, even as government watchdogs continued to document serious deficiencies.

Meyer said Hegseth has made the issue a personal priority.

"We have the secretary of war who is putting people first, and he's not just saying that. He's doing it through his actions," Meyer said.

Meyer has put his own name on whether the latest effort succeeds, saying previously that if the barracks aren't fixed, there is "only one person to blame" — himself.

Asked what "fixed" would actually look like, Meyer offered a simpler standard than any Pentagon metric.

"People are living in places that I would be OK for my daughters living in," he said.

#6069. Trump Has Shifted the U.S.-Pakistan Relationship

South Asia Brief: Trump Has Shifted the U.S.-Pakistan Relationship

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: A proposed liquefied natural gas project in Pakistan underscores close ties with the Trump administration, garment workers in Bangladesh protest for pay increases, and India’s opposition alliance rallies to call for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: A proposed liquefied natural gas project in Pakistan underscores close ties with the Trump administration, garment workers in Bangladesh protest for pay increases, and India’s opposition alliance rallies to call for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, Pakistan has banked heavily on doing business with the United States. With the Democrats flipping both houses of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, though, one has to wonder if Islamabad could come out as another loser.

For one thing, scrutiny of Trump’s business dealings will certainly increase, constraining his administration’s capacity to pursue deals abroad.

A big topic of discussion in Pakistan this week—along with the midterms—is the news that a consortium of U.S. companies has proposed a $4.4 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Port Qasim, near Karachi. It would be Pakistan’s first LNG storage facility, helping to shield the country from global energy shocks.

The proposal entails a large-scale storage terminal and eventually a 680-mile delivery pipeline. The plan is backed by the U.S. Trade and Development Agency, U.S. International Development Finance Corp., and the Export-Import Bank of the United States.

Washington’s support for the proposed LNG project underscores just how much the U.S.-Pakistan relationship has changed in Trump’s second term. Bilateral ties were downgraded after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, in large part because Washington had long viewed relations with Islamabad through a security lens.

The Trump administration turned this approach on its head. The United States now prioritizes ties with Pakistan, and Trump often praises the country’s leadership. Though counterterrorism still figures in the relationship, Washington has emphasized economic and commercial issues in its engagement with Islamabad.

In particular, the United States has taken a strong interest in Pakistan’s critical minerals and cryptocurrency resources. It has pushed for the country to import more U.S. goods, including energy supplies. In October 2025, Pakistan received its first-ever shipment of U.S. crude oil. Washington has pushed to remove trade obstacles with Islamabad, including ending a two-year ban on U.S. soybean exports.

Pakistan, which had long pitched its economic offerings to the United States unsuccessfully, has capitalized on the Trump administration’s newfound interest in its assets. The Financial Times reported last year that Islamabad went as far as to offer Washington the opportunity to build and manage a port on the Arabian Sea. (Pakistan publicly denies this.)

The proposed LNG project would be one of the Trump administration’s most ambitious commercial ventures in Pakistan, perhaps putting an exclamation point on the shift in the U.S. approach to the country. Yet that shift might not even be sustainable—especially given the midterm results.

The Trump administration’s commercial focus is largely driven by the president’s whims and by the economic interests of his family members and close associates. But this arrangement won’t outlast Trump’s term, which ends in two years. Further, with Congress in the hands of the Democrats starting in January, it could also become more difficult to pull off.

Conversations with Pakistani interlocutors this week revealed a combination of curiosity and concern about ties with the United States in the Trump era. There seems to be a desire to understand how the relationship improved so quickly alongside a sense that it might not last for long, given Trump’s unpredictability. The Democrats’ victory will only sharpen these concerns.

These worries reflect an evergreen challenge for the U.S.-Pakistan relationship: how to craft a strong partnership that can withstand political change in both countries and weather external shocks.

The last time the White House officially announced a policy on Pakistan was during Trump’s first term, in August 2017, when a new South Asia strategy included a hard-line approach toward Islamabad. It’s clear that the United States is overdue in conducting a formal review of its Pakistan policy, even as the relationship is being informally reevaluated and refashioned.

Garment protests in Bangladesh. Garment workers have taken to the streets in industrial areas of Dhaka, Bangladesh’s capital, in recent days to call for pay increases. Clashes with security forces have prompted the closure of dozens of garment factories and raised concerns about shipment delays.

Garment workers are a critical constituency in Bangladesh, numbering around 4 million, and the sector accounts for 80 percent of the country’s export earnings. Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry is a global success story; it made the country one of South Asia’s best-performing economies until a slump in the last few years.

With the downturn, Bangladesh seems to be paying the price for relying so heavily on a single export—as globally competitive as it was—for so long. The protests are just the latest policy challenge for Dhaka, which is already struggling with economic stress, energy shortages, and the world’s most serious measles crisis.

These issues risk distracting Bangladesh from pursuing economic and governance reforms—something the government, which took office in February, was given a mandate to prioritize.

India’s opposition alliance rallies. On Sunday, the main opposition alliance in India staged protests in New Delhi to call for the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The rally drew tens of thousands of people and marked the latest mobilization against a voter roll revision that critics say favored the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party has spearheaded the protests calling for Kumar to step down. This summer, the Cockroach movement galvanized protests over leaked exam papers that ultimately resulted in the resignation of the country’s education minister.

Now, India’s opposition is riding on the coattails of this activism. The success of the Cockroach movement is a gift to the opposition, which has long been hobbled by the absence of a popular leader and disagreements within its alliance.

Heat stress becomes serious vulnerability. The International Labor Organization (ILO) released studies last week warning that by 2040, workplace heat stress spawned by rising temperatures could lead to reduced working time equivalent to around 145,000 full-time jobs in Sri Lanka and 2,400 in the Maldives.

The reports estimate that these losses will be valued at around $26 billion in Sri Lanka and $576 million in the Maldives. The hardest-hit sector in Sri Lanka will be agriculture, along with services, manufacturing, and construction. In the Maldives, services and construction will be the most vulnerable industries.

The ILO findings are a reminder of the high economic cost of climate change in a region where economies are fragile—and where some of the most labor-dependent sectors are especially vulnerable to climate effects.

Last Sunday, around 200,000 people converged on the Bhutanese town of Gelephu to watch volunteers construct 108 stupas. (The number 108 is sacred in Buddhism.) The initiative is part of a campaign led by Bhutan’s king to transform Gelephu, near Bhutan’s border with India, into a “mindfulness city.”

Bhutan hopes to use the initiative, which emphasizes ecological sustainability and happiness, as an antidote to the country’s deepening economic stress. The stupa project is certainly an unorthodox way to tackle these problems. Critics will likely say it does little to reverse rising unemployment and a rapid outflow of highly skilled workers.

However, the project aligns with a long-standing Bhutanese principle known as “gross national happiness,” which measures national well-being not by income or other economic indicators but instead by the level of contentment among citizens.

Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. X: @michaelkugelman

#6068. Talarico, Hinojosa win big in Texas despite Elon Musk’s millions

James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

This marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a new record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

Although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

Although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

#6067. GOP eyes Senate comeback after Democratic bloodbath, but another political nightmare could await

The 2026 midterm elections result in a political shift as Democrats are projected to take control of the U.S. House and Senate. Fox News host Jesse Watters breaks down the major Democratic victories.

Republican control of the Senate could return as soon as the 2028 general election, but only if the party can pull off a series of crucial victories in competitive races, a possibility that seems distant following Tuesday night's devastating Democratic sweep.

As of publication, Democrats and independents who caucus with them have secured 54 Senate seats, a total that could grow to as many as 56 pending election calls in Mississippi and Alaska.

Assuming Republicans hold the vice presidency in 2028, far from a guarantee, they would need to flip at least four seats during that election cycle to win the Senate back.

While there are ample pickup opportunities for Republicans in 2028 if the party can return to its typical national performance benchmarks, several vulnerable GOP-held seats could complicate their efforts to retake the upper chamber.

DEMS FLIPS YET ANOTHER SENATE SEAT IN TRUMP COUNTRY AMID SWEEPING GOP UPSETS

The U.S. Capitol on Dec.12, 2024 (Fox News/Paul Steinhauser)

Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, for instance, turned 93 in September and faces a decision about whether to seek another term in 2028, when Republicans will be defending his seat in a state where Democrat Josh Turek just defeated Republican Ashley Hinson by roughly four percentage points. His departure before then could also give Iowa's incoming Democratic governor the opportunity to appoint a temporary replacement.

Another possibility that could make the GOP's path back to a majority even more uncertain is the admission of Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., to the union as full states.

Such a move would likely require the Democratic-led Senate to abolish or overcome the legislative filibuster, something lawmakers representing more moderate or competitive states may balk at, as well as support in the House and either presidential approval or enough votes to override a veto.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

The proposal comes as Republicans seek to convince voters that keeping the GOP in power would translate into more money in Americans' pockets. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Even if the filibuster is done away with, President Donald Trump could veto admittance bills. Democrats currently lack the numbers to override such a veto.

If Republicans lose the White House in 2028, however, Democrats could have a clearer path to advancing statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., a move that would add four Senate seats and potentially complicate Republican efforts to win back the chamber, though significant political and legal obstacles would remain.

Assuming none of that happens, Democrats will be defending six Senate seats that could offer Republicans potential pickup opportunities in 2028.

Republicans will have pickup opportunities in New Hampshire, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio that year. They will, however, be forced to defend vulnerable Senate seats in Wisconsin, Iowa and North Carolina.

Indiana, which saw a significant blue shift, also has a Senate seat up for contention in 2028, while Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn mounted a competitive but unsuccessful challenge to Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts on Tuesday, will not hold another regularly scheduled Senate election until 2030.

While 2028 could deliver Republicans a majority if they play their cards right, another defeat on the scale of 2026 could put the Democratic Party dangerously close to the 60-vote threshold necessary to invoke cloture and counter a filibuster.

"It may be unlikely, but I do think it's feasible," Chip Wyatt, Heritage Action's government relations director, told Fox News Digital. "We're just as capable of having a night like the Democrats had on Tuesday in 2028.

"If anything, that election, the election we had on Tuesday, has shown us that two years is a very, very long time in politics. I think if you had told anybody in 2024 that this is what happened in 2028, they probably wouldn't believe you."

For Republicans to have a good night in 2028, Wyatt argued that conservatives would have to focus on affordability issues while Democrats overstep their mandate by allowing the fringes of their party to dictate its policy agenda.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz took a similar line in reacting to Tuesday night's election results.

"We will rebuild as a true blue-collar party, not by embracing socialism, but by being real free-market conservatives, the way we built the Texas economic miracle in the first place, and we will build and rebuild America as well," he said.

"When the zealots overreach, and they will, we will stand ready to lead in the direction of freedom, of prosperity, of safety and security and common sense. We will return to a new dawn of freedom in America."

The year 2030 features slightly fewer pickups for the GOP with a comparable number of states to defend. While Republicans will have pickup opportunities in Arizona, Nevada, Wisconsin and Michigan, they will also be forced to defend seats in Texas, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa and chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, speaks during a hearing in Washington Sept. 16, 2025 (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The 2032 election will feature the same regularly scheduled Senate seats contested in 2026, giving Republicans another opportunity to retake deep-red states they blundered this year, such as Kansas and South Carolina. Historically, however, some moderate Democrats have managed to hang on to statewide offices in typically red states, making a reversion far from a certainty.

Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin, for instance, managed to survive multiple GOP challenges in the deep-red state. Kansas and Kentucky, similarly, have Democratic governors that survived Republican challenges in races that received national attention.

While many Republicans, and even some Democrats, have suggested liberal pickups in deep red states could be one-cycle wonders, Wyatt cautioned against complacency.

"We should always assume the politicians want to get re-elected, and, so, the senators in the deep red states that have been recently elected as Democrats are going to want to keep their seats. And, so, they're going to be very strategic in how they vote and in what kind of bills they're introducing," Wyatt said.

"In some of these deep red states, it's going to be difficult for [Democrats] to hold on to these seats. ... Now, granted, I've already said two years is a long time, six years is an even longer time.

"So, who knows what kind of political landscape we're looking at in 2032, but Republicans should definitely start off with a strong advantage in many of these states. ... But it's never wise to counter chickens before they hatch."

Electoral politics is famously unpredictable. Nobody in 2024, for instance, envisioned South Carolina or Kansas sending Democrats to the Senate in 2026. It is possible that the Republican path to a Senate majority, or lack thereof, will be comparably surprising.

#6063. Americans Care About Foreign Policy. Now Democrats Must Listen to Them.

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Americans Care About Foreign Policy. Now Democrats Must Listen to Them.

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

There is a trope of U.S. political journalism so time-tested as to nearly rise to the level of a verity: In making their choices, voters in the United States place little emphasis on foreign affairs. But yesterday’s overwhelming victory by opposition Democrats has proved that this falls well short of a rule.

One needn’t take this on my authority. On Wednesday morning, after picking through the disastrous results for his Republican Party, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … [E]veryone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

There is a trope of U.S. political journalism so time-tested as to nearly rise to the level of a verity: In making their choices, voters in the United States place little emphasis on foreign affairs. But yesterday’s overwhelming victory by opposition Democrats has proved that this falls well short of a rule.

One needn’t take this on my authority. On Wednesday morning, after picking through the disastrous results for his Republican Party, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … [E]veryone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Vance was attributing a clarity to his boss that U.S. President Donald Trump has shied from exhibiting on the United States and Israel’s ill-conceived and poorly executed war against Iran, which many observers believe was largely inspired by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Israeli leader has long sought to persuade U.S. presidents to attack Iran, and in Trump, he finally found a willing—or gullible—partner.

As is well understood by now, Trump and Netanyahu’s war against Iran failed according to nearly all of its many shifting rationales. It did not destroy Iran’s Islamic system of government. It did not permanently defeat Tehran’s regional ambitions and may not even have downsized them. Iran still maintains extensive control over the supply of oil to global markets through the Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies, the Houthis, have demonstrated not just persistence but surprising prowess in attacking Saudi Arabia and other key Arab allies and arms clients of the United States.

But this is only the beginning of the pain that this war has incurred for the United States. Perhaps the single biggest factor in the elections, it has driven up U.S. gasoline and diesel prices far above their prewar levels, and in doing so, it has stoked inflation and driven up interest rates, creating hardship for tens of millions of Americans.

Skeptics may say this simply confirms the old wisdom that Americans only care about foreign affairs when it costs them money. But that is a distinction without much difference. Voters were not confused about the cause of their hardship. As Vance himself acknowledged, they knew it was the war.

This conflict, which was unquestionably a war of choice that many Americans see as having been unnecessary, has also badly depleted many of Washington’s most capable and expensive munitions, weakening its military posture in the world’s most sensitive theaters: the East China Sea and both Ukraine and NATO’s borderlands with Russia.

Combined with the extended deployment of aircraft carrier battle groups in the Middle East, this depletion has left both Taiwan and islands disputed between Beijing and Tokyo more vulnerable than at any time in recent memory to Chinese attack. Meanwhile, even if Trump were able to wake up from the trance that Russian President Vladimir Putin seems to have put him in, Washington now has far fewer of the advanced weapons systems that Kyiv desperately needs to defend itself from Moscow’s indiscriminate missile and drone attacks.

Beyond the midterms, foreign policy is likely to remain on center stage in the struggle between Trump and Congress over the next two years. Presidents who lose one or both chambers of Congress during midterm elections almost always face a sharp limitation in their powers. It is the rare administration that is able to pass any major domestic legislation under these circumstances. And so lame ducks tend to focus their energies on foreign policy, an arena in which the Constitution grants presidents tremendous sway.

At the same time, Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives are unlikely to be able to pass any major reforms that the president will sign into law. Like Trump, these legislators may find that some of their greatest opportunities to affect U.S. policy and the country’s place in the world relate to international affairs.

Their first priority, given that it was a campaign promise across congressional races, will be to end the conflict with Iran. But how to do so from Capitol Hill? The answer lies in stringent control of the budget and enforcing the kind of accountability that was totally abandoned by the pliant, outgoing Republican Congress. Trump is seeking a vast increase in military spending, and the incoming Congress has the power to make sure that extending the war in Iran will not be funded.

This will not be easy. Congress has almost always found it difficult to resist new spending requests for the Pentagon. But this Congress, and its Democratic leaders, will be judged in good part on its ability to rein in Trump in the Middle East. That will require sorting through military appropriations with a fine-toothed comb and holding hearings that seek to extract clarity from the president’s military and foreign-policy appointees to an unaccustomed degree.

The bombastic and ill-prepared U.S. defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, is the most obvious target here. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio should receive equal attention. So far, he has been supremely slippery in terms of evading frank and detailed discussion of the Iran war, and that must end now.

If Iran sits atop the list of foreign-policy priorities for the new Congress, though, it nonetheless has serious competition. The Democrats can and must bring about badly needed accountability in other areas as well. Here, I’ll start with the United States’ increasingly grotesque collusion with Russia in its war on Ukraine. This has recently gone beyond limiting arms supplies to Kyiv and potentially hindering satellite intelligence through Elon Musk’s Starlink system that Ukraine badly needs for defense. Now, it includes casting a succession of economic lifelines to Moscow through oil deals with Russia and pressure on Europe to restore Russian energy supplies.

Congress will also have a vital role to play in achieving transparency in the White House’s smash-and-grab coup in Venezuela, in which it abducted a sitting president, installed a client to lead the country, and then secured opaque arrangements for Washington and U.S. private interests in Venezuela’s vast, if decrepit, oil industry.

More broadly, Trump has ridden roughshod over relations with advanced industrial allies all over the world, from Canada to Japan to South Korea. Meanwhile, he has turned the country’s back on the so-called developing world, displaying a crude disregard for the fellow humanity of people in poorer countries, many of whom once looked up to the United States. At a minimum, Congress must lay bare the sheer incoherence and self-destruction at work in these Trump policies in areas from economic growth to mutual defense to global public health.

Lastly, I come to Israel, not because it is the least of these topics, but because it may be the most difficult. Democrats will have to reckon with their own divisions before they can reckon with the wrongheadedness of overall U.S. foreign policy toward the country. Yet the time has come for the United States to stop indulging Israel’s worst behavior, including the genocidal atrocities of its campaign in Gaza and the settler violence and growing dispossession of Palestinians in the West Bank.

Trump himself tried to get ahead of this issue on the day of the election by saying that the United States will no longer massively underwrite Israel’s defense, as it has done for decades, and sell Israel the arms that it needs instead. But much more is required.

The United States has long been more a willing than unwitting partner of Israel in the destruction of Palestinian communities. It play-acted around dedication to a two-state solution for years prior to the Trump administration, which simply dropped the mask and ceased even pretending to care about the fate of Palestinians.

Democrats know that growing popular disenchantment with Israel’s heedless violence was a significant factor in this week’s victory. Now they must get over the notion, still popular in many quarters, that to forthrightly criticize Israel’s behavior and hold this long-standing U.S. ally to account constitutes antisemitism. In fact, treating Israel with respect demands this. And so will the preservation of the U.S.-Israeli alliance.

On Israel, as on Iran, voters have moved faster than the Washington consensus. The old truism held that Americans do not vote on foreign policy. This week they did, and the Democrats they elected should take them at their word.

#6062. Democratic senator-elect calls Trump 'unserious fool' while defending combative political style

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed mocked Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump in his victory speech.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, leaned into accusations of acting cocky on the path to victory over Republican candidate Mike Rogers, citing a need to push back on President Donald Trump’s manner of communication during an appearance on "Pod Save America."

"Long ago, you predicted that you would win this race by seven points, which, at the time, seemed like a pretty cocky and ill-considered thing to say. Then you won the race by seven points. People are still calling you cocky," podcast host Jon Favreau said during his interview with El-Sayed.

"I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed replied.

EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

El-Sayed’s response sheds light on his view of his own campaign and the tone that he believes Democrats need to adopt to counter Trump’s presence in American politics. It also raises questions of whether El-Sayed’s campaign strategies will yield results in Congress.

In his view, Trump has changed the style of acceptable communication. In turn, he accused Democrats of being hesitant to abandon a kind of decorum to fight fire with fire.

"I just think there’s a responsibility for us to walk out of 'The West Wing' episode that our politics used to feel like and into the reality of where we are," El-Sayed said, referring to a television drama known for its idealistic portrayal of American politics.

"I say that because if you’ve ever watched a bully in a room, if you don’t stand up to the bully, it’s not like the bully will just go away. The bully just gets stronger."

President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena Oct. 30, 2026, in Daytona Beach, Fla. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller outside the White House Oct. 6, 2025. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

#6057. Palestinian Voters Gave Eisenkot a Chance to Govern—He Should Take It

Argument: Palestinian Voters Gave Eisenkot a Chance to Govern—He Should Take It

Much of the analysis since Israel’s election on Oct. 27 has described the result as a deadlock—a stalemate between the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot. According to this framing, neither side managed to clinch a majority in the 120-member parliament, with Netanyahu and his satellite parties mustering 53 seats and Eisenkot and his bloc capturing 48. As a result, Israel now finds itself at a political impasse.

But this conclusion is based on faulty arithmetic. It fails to take into account the single most striking aspect of the election: the fact that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up roughly 20 percent of the population, voted in unprecedented numbers, helping two Palestinian-led parties capture a record 19 parliamentary seats. Their votes were an explicit repudiation of Netanyahu and his policies, which means that their representatives in parliament should be counted as part of the opposition bloc—bringing the tally to 67 seats. By any objective accounting, this is not a deadlock; it’s a win for the opposition, or at least, it should be framed as such.

Much of the analysis since Israel’s election on Oct. 27 has described the result as a deadlock—a stalemate between the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot. According to this framing, neither side managed to clinch a majority in the 120-member parliament, with Netanyahu and his satellite parties mustering 53 seats and Eisenkot and his bloc capturing 48. As a result, Israel now finds itself at a political impasse.

But this conclusion is based on faulty arithmetic. It fails to take into account the single most striking aspect of the election: the fact that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up roughly 20 percent of the population, voted in unprecedented numbers, helping two Palestinian-led parties capture a record 19 parliamentary seats. Their votes were an explicit repudiation of Netanyahu and his policies, which means that their representatives in parliament should be counted as part of the opposition bloc—bringing the tally to 67 seats. By any objective accounting, this is not a deadlock; it’s a win for the opposition, or at least, it should be framed as such.

High voter turnout, especially from within a minority community that is constantly accused of being rejectionist, is what one hopes for in a healthy democracy. It reflects a collective determination to participate in the electoral process and assume ownership over the decisions and institutions that shape people’s lives. Americans can only envy such high turnout.

But Israel is a country that prioritizes Jewish citizens and their rights over Palestinians. This is enshrined the 2018 Jewish nation-state law, which lays out the right to national self-determination solely for Jews. It’s also a country that largely treats Palestinian Israeli parliament members as external to the governing system. In Israel’s 78-year history, a Palestinian-led party has been included in a governing coalition only once, for just a yearlong period.

So when the exit polls started to come in on election night, and it became clear that Palestinian Israelis were instrumental in blocking a majority for another Netanyahu coalition, Eisenkot— the leader of the largest opposition party—did nothing to signal that the two Palestinian-led parties would be welcome in his coalition. He has maintained that posture in the days since the vote.

Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc does not speak in one voice on this issue. One member of the bloc, a left-wing party known as the Democrats and headed by Yair Golan, has welcomed the idea of a governing partnership with the Palestinian-led parties. But two other parties have ruled it out.

There are, of course, ideological and political differences among the Palestinian-led parties. One of them, the Joint List, is an amalgam of three different factions, and it tends to focus on the big diplomatic issues, including ending Israel’s war in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank and advancing equality for Palestinian Israelis. The Joint List won 11 seats in the election. Its rival is the United Arab List or Raam, which prioritizes bread-and-butter issues, including securing larger allocations for its constituencies and ending home demolitions. The United Arab List, which captured eight seats, served in a governing coalition for one year, in 2021.

But opposition leaders—along with much of the Israeli media and, of course, Netanyahu himself—broadly blur those distinctions, lumping all Palestinian Arab parties together in a blanket rejection and ignoring their electoral power. Netanyahu and others have also incited against them by describing them as terror supporters.

Naftali Bennett’s Beyachad party and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu—the two opposition factions that oppose partnering with the Palestinian-led parties—argue that to do so would be unpalatable to Jewish Israelis in the aftermath of the Hamas attack of Oct. 7, 2023. This claim ignores the fact that Palestinian citizens were also killed and abducted in the Hamas attack, were also part of the rescue services that saved lives, and also suffered heavy missile fire in the ensuing years of war (with their communities often lacking sufficient shelter). This, in addition to the fact that they are facing the worst wave of homicides on record due to unchecked organized crime—one of the issues that drove them to vote out the Netanyahu government.

Pollster Dahlia Scheindlin on whether Benjamin Netanyahu can stay in power.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Even as Palestinian citizens have been shunned and excluded from Israel’s political spaces, this election has demonstrated that they remain omnipresent, relevant, and consequential to the country’s future. The importance of the vote lies in what it has exposed: that Israel’s insistence on being a Jewish and democratic state doesn’t hold if you continue ignoring and disenfranchising Palestinian citizens; that doing so has real implications for Israel’s already-flawed democracy and its commitment to civil rights; and, crucially, that without the support of Palestinian Israelis, it appears to be largely impossible for Jewish Israelis to unseat Netanyahu and move past his politics of war and intransigence.

The insistence on dividing Israelis along ethnic and religious, rather than civic and political lines, is self-defeating if you want a change in power that is centered on policies, not identity. Some Israelis are increasingly coming to understand this. According to one survey conducted days after the election, a solid majority of opposition voters said that if forced to choose, they preferred a minority government that rests on the support of the United Arab List over a broad-based government with Netanyahu or another snap election.

It remains a question whether Eisenkot will decide to break the taboo and normalize the Palestinian parties. He has specified four demands that any partner must meet to join a coalition: accepting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, recognizing the foundational values of the Declaration of Independence, committing to mandatory national service for all (military or civilian), and declaring that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be eliminated. These are tough conditions, but they leave at least some small room for maneuvering on both sides.

One possibility would be for Eisenkot to form a minority government with some Palestinian Israeli lawmakers while relying on the support or abstention of others during key parliamentary votes. This could allow the sides to cooperate without compromising their platforms. And it would help all opposition leaders keep their core promise to voters to oust Netanyahu from office.

Such a government could well be unstable and short-lived. But by taking a clear stance in favor of partnering with Palestinian Israeli parties, Eisenkot would be spearheading a shift in Israeli politics, one that could well impact future elections. Such a government would also be a clear repudiation of the racist, divisive, and anti-democratic zeitgeist personified and epitomized by Netanyahu, who has been trying to undermine the election results.

Some cooperation could take place even before a new coalition is formed. Once the new members of parliament are sworn in on Nov. 10, Eisenkot has a majority in the house—with the help of the Palestinian Israeli parties—to elect a new speaker of the parliament. The speaker could help shape a new legislative agenda and begin to advance the issues on which the opposition campaigned—including establishing a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the Oct. 7 attack and annulling the highly controversial and illiberal judicial overhaul laws.

This would allow the new parliament to assume some powers from the Netanyahu coalition, even as he remains the caretaker prime minister with his ministers still in place. It would cement Eisenkot as a bold and competent leader who can deliver on the will of the majority while signaling to Netanyahu that, in this transitional period, he does not have carte blanche to engage in another unprovoked war, whether in Iran or elsewhere.

And it would recognize the rights of the members of Israel’s Palestinian minority, who took it upon themselves to try to change their futures within the bounds and systems of an Israeli state that has repeatedly rejected them and discriminated against them. That’s a win-win.

Mairav Zonszein is the senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group. She has written for the New York Times, the Washington Post, and the Columbia Journalism Review, among others. X: @MairavZ
