#6052. Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

This article was originally published on The Conversation.

Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later said, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as âreduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.â

The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like âspontaneous morning erectionsâ as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administrationâs tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call âcringe fascism.â

For some time thereâs been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trumpâs presidency could be considered âfascist.â Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

And thatâs where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,âcringeâ is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesnât seem to be to them.

For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing â or cringe.

But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegsethâs testosterone policy, hides a much more serious â and to some critics, fascist â reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

As Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trumpâs authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. Thatâs especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trumpâs inner circle.

Consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of âblood and soilâ in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to âDefend the Homeland.â

And then there are the attacks on the press as the âenemy of the people,â echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trumpâs banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoevenâs âStarship Troopers,â in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid âcringe.â

Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

On the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on menâs bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Hustedâs rear feels deeply surreal.

Trumpâs seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

It is difficult to see criticsâ view of Trumpâs second term as âfascistâ when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

Is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trumpâs supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that â as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia shows â regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet thatâs why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison

#6051. Republican state lawmakers reported Omar to the IRS in 2019

Chad Pergram reports on Capitol Hill regarding the reopened investigation into Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2009 marriage to Ahmed Elmi.

EXCLUSIVE: A group of Minnesota Republican state lawmakers asked the IRS in August 2019 to "conduct a detailed reexamination" of tax filings by Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., based on a report from a state board suggesting she filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 with a man she was not legally married to, according to a letter obtained by Fox News Digital.

The letter was sent after the Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board issued a report June 6, 2019, indicating Omar had filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 with Ahmed Hirsi despite being legally married to another man, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, at the time.

The joint tax returns came up during the Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board’s examination of a $1,500 expense associated with Omar’s campaign committee.

The board was investigating whether the expenditure was a legitimate campaign-related expense or whether campaign funds had been used to pay for services that benefited Omar personally. The payment was part of a larger $2,250 reimbursement to the Kjellberg Law Office for legal and other services.

In 2019, a group of Minnesota Republican state lawmakers asked the IRS to investigate tax filings by Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. (Adam Gray/AP Photo)

ILHAN OMAR ISSUES STUNNING ADMISSION WHEN CONFRONTED WITH BROTHER MARRIAGE RUMORS

In response to the board’s questions, Omar’s campaign committee explained that the Kjellberg Law Office had retained the accounting firm Frederick & Rosen to obtain and review financial records as part of the campaign committee’s efforts to respond to allegations about Omar’s marital history.

According to the committee’s explanation, Frederick & Rosen prepared releases for Omar and Ahmed Hirsi to sign, so the firm could obtain copies of their filed joint federal income tax returns for 2014 and 2015 from the IRS.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., continues to generate headlines related to her finances. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

The board concluded that the committee had not demonstrated that the $1,500 expense benefited the campaign and required Omar to reimburse the committee.

JD VANCE SAYS DOJ LOOKING INTO IF ILHAN OMAR COMMITTED IMMIGRATION FRAUD AMID BROTHER-MARRIAGE ALLEGATIONS

Omar married Hirsi in 2002 in their Muslim faith tradition, and they ended their relationship in that tradition in 2008, Newsweek reported. She then legally married Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in February 2009, according to public records, as reported by Newsweek.

According to divorce documents obtained by Fox News Digital, Omar legally divorced Elmi in December 2017.

Carla Kjellberg, a lawyer for Omar and her campaign committee, stated during the board proceedings that Frederick & Rosen’s services provided "some personal benefit to Rep. Omar," because "there was an issue with her tax returns that needed to be corrected regardless of her status as a candidate," according to the board’s report.

In a letter to then-IRS Commissioner Charles Rettig dated Aug. 6, 2019, the state lawmakers asked the IRS to undertake a review in light of the Minnesota Campaign Finance Board report.

"Due to recent developments, I believe probable cause exists for an investigation into Rep. Omar's tax filings," the letter, signed by Minnesota state Reps. Steve Drazkowski, Linda Runbeck, Glenn Gruenhagen, Shane Mekeland, John Poston, Eric Lucero, Duane Quam, Tim Miller, Cal Bahr and Jeremy Munson, said.

Drazkowski told Fox News Digital the IRS never responded to the request.

The IRS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Fox News Digital could not confirm whether the IRS followed through with the lawmakers’ request.

Federal tax confidentiality rules generally restrict what the agency can disclose about individual taxpayers. The Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board issued its findings on June 6, 2019, after two complaints filed by Drazkowski.

Although the board required Omar to repay the $1,500 that her campaign had paid the Kjellberg Law Firm for Frederick & Rosen’s services related to the tax returns, it rejected the allegation that this money was payment for Omar’s personal divorce proceeding, in which Kjellberg also represented her.

The board also required Omar to repay campaign funds used for certain travel expenses, including trips to Boston, New York and Washington, D.C.

After the board's 2019 findings, Omar said she was "glad" the process was complete and welcomed the board's determination regarding allegations that she had improperly used campaign funds for personal expenses. However, she did not address the portion of the board’s report concerning the joint tax returns she submitted with Hirsi.

Omar did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

In a separate letter obtained by Fox News Digital, the Republican state lawmakers, led by Drazkowski, asked Cynthia Bauerly, then the commissioner of the Minnesota Department of Revenue, in August 2019 to review Omar's joint tax filings.

Drazkowski said neither Bauerly nor the Minnesota Department of Revenue responded to the lawmakers' request.

The Minnesota Department of Revenue did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The letter from the lawmakers urging the state and federal tax reporting agencies to investigate Omar’s joint tax filings came two months after Drazkowski urged Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., to refer his concerns about Omar's tax filings to the House Ethics Committee.

As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Craig told Drazkowski in a letter he could submit information himself to the Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), which was renamed to the Office of Congressional Conduct in 2021.

Ilhan Omar with Ahmed Hirsi in 2018. (Kerem Yucel/AFP via Getty Images)

The congressional ethics process allows members of the public and lawmakers to submit information concerning alleged misconduct, although the independent ethics office and the House Committee on Ethics have separate procedures.

In late October, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News the federal investigation into Omar regarding potential immigration and marriage fraud had been referred to the Department of Justice as a "large case" that targets multiple individuals rather than just one person.

The DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on whether the investigation is looking into the 2014 and 2015 joint tax filings flagged by the state lawmakers in 2019.

Soon, images of Mansouri meeting with the king, both of them dressed in traditional outfits of the same light-blue shade, circulated around the world. It’s a moment that would have been unimaginable not so long ago.

On Sept. 29, King Mohammed VI named Fatima Ezzahra Mansouri as Morocco’s head of government, making the country the second in the Arab world after Tunisia to appoint a woman to lead its executive branch. Soon, images of Mansouri meeting with the king, both of them dressed in traditional outfits of the same light-blue shade, circulated around the world. It’s a moment that would have been unimaginable not so long ago.

Mansouri’s appointment brought excitement to an otherwise uneventful election that was largely ignored by many Moroccans. The vote, which took place on Sept. 23, had an abstention rate of almost 62 percent, the country’s highest in almost 20 years. The low turnout was the culmination of decades-long apathy toward elections, with citizens feeling increasingly disconnected from Morocco’s political parties.

Yet while Mansouri’s new role is symbolically important, she will have limited power, as executive authority rests with the king. Still, her leadership comes at a pivotal moment for the country, and she will have a chance to influence issues that are important to many citizens, including the much-anticipated reform of Morocco’s family status law. If she succeeds in shaping policies that improve Moroccans’ lives and support gender equality, she may very well leave her mark on a country that is striving to modernize even as it has long leaned conservative.

Mansouri’s nomination has not been particularly surprising to observers of Moroccan politics. Although women historically did not hold key government positions, that has started to change over the last three decades. In 1993, the first two women were elected to the House of Representatives. Women have also occupied more government roles since 2000, when the late Zoulikha Nasri became the first female royal advisor to the king. Currently, although women still lag in political representation, 107 of the House’s 395 seats are filled by women.

Moroccan women have also become increasingly prominent in civil society. In 2007, the Moroccan Association of Human Rights (AMDH), perhaps the region’s most influential rights organization, elected its first woman president, Khadija Ryadi. (It is currently led by another woman, Souad Brahma.) Five years later, Nabila Mounib became the first elected female secretary-general of a political party, the Unified Socialist Party (PSU). And the National Human Rights Council, whose leaders are appointed by the king, has been led by Amina Bouayach since 2018.

These trends have coincided with Morocco’s transition to a more democratic constitutional monarchy. Before the Arab Spring, the king could choose anyone he wished to be prime minister. This changed after the “February 20 Movement” demonstrations in 2011 shook the country, leading to democratic practices taking root. The new 2011 constitution enshrined gender equality and gave more power to the prime minister—now called the head of government—and parliament. Morocco’s king now has to choose a head of government from the party that wins the general election, though he maintains control over certain divisions of government, such as the ministries of the interior and foreign affairs.

In the lead-up to this year’s election, the possibility of Mansouri’s nomination loomed over the end of the campaign, because she is a prominent figure in the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which was widely expected to win. A liberal party that describes itself as “modernist,” the PAM was created in 2008 by current royal advisor Fouad Ali El Himma, and many Moroccans have since associated it with the country’s real decisionmakers in the royal palace. Its political purpose was to rival the Islamist party, the Justice and Development Party (PJD). The PJD led Morocco’s coalition governments from 2011 to 2021, when it suffered a major defeat. In September, the PAM won 97 seats, securing a major victory, though it had to form a coalition to govern.

Mansouri, who is 50 years old, is no newcomer to politics. Her father, Abderrahmane El Mansouri, led the Marrakech bar association, served as the city’s “pasha,” a high-ranking city administrator, and later became Morocco’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates. She followed in his footsteps, becoming a lawyer before moving into politics. In 2007, she joined the Mouvement de tous les démocrates, which laid the groundwork for the PAM. Since then, she has become one of the PAM’s three leaders, and at the time of her appointment, she was serving as both mayor of Marrakech and Morocco’s housing minister.

Mansouri is not known as an outspoken women’s rights advocate, though she openly celebrated her appointment as a historic event and a victory for Moroccan women in her first declaration as head of government. And of the new government’s 32 ministers, only six are women, including Mansouri. Nevertheless, when it comes to women’s rights, the political elite has sent a clear message: Soon after her nomination, many possible political allies in her coalition government expressed their support for a woman occupying the role.

While Mansouri will have only limited room for decision-making, she will still play an important role in the coming months as Rabat tries to find its footing and implement highly anticipated reforms in a delicate political climate.

First, she will oversee new reforms to the Moudawana, or family status law, which is an extremely sensitive topic in Moroccan politics. The Moudawana law is inspired by Islamic principles and concerns issues such as women’s rights, child custody, and the legal age of marriage. The law underwent major revisions in 2004, in a process that sparked significant societal tensions. In recent years, King Mohammed VI has called for another reform, which will address inflammatory subjects such as divorce and equality in inheritance rights, which Moroccan conservatives and Islamists will surely oppose.

It will take political courage for Mansouri to modernize the Moudawana, as she will certainly face considerable opposition. But how she approaches it will impact Moroccan society for decades and represents a unique opportunity to enact radical change for gender equality.

In addition, Morocco’s government will have to manage co-hosting the 2030 FIFA World Cup amid deep socioeconomic tensions. Last fall, the country was shaken by the Gen Z 212 protests, a movement that called for investment in education and health reforms instead of the billions of dollars slated for building and modernizing soccer stadiums. This led to a wave of detention, with some 2,500 people prosecuted—at least 580 of whom are currently incarcerated, according to Omar Arbib of AMDH.

Mansouri will also have to tackle the related issues of the high cost of living and youth disillusionment, illustrated by more than 70,000 Moroccans fleeing to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July. (Most have since been returned, and at least 145 have died.)

Although Morocco boasts strong GDP growth of around 4 percent, according to the High Commission for Planning, many citizens aged 15 to 24 have been largely left behind, with a 30 percent unemployment rate. Moreover, 3 million Moroccans between the ages of 15 and 29 are characterized as NEET (Not in Employment, Education, or Training), and many young Moroccans show political apathy; 18- to 24-year-olds account for 12 percent of the population but just 4 percent of the country’s 15.8 million registered voters.

So far, Moroccans have been largely in a state of anticipation. “Let’s see what she does, and then we’ll judge,” has been a common refrain over the last few weeks. Some young people I spoke to approve of Mansouri because of her gender but added that it wasn’t “the woman of their choice.” (They would have preferred Mounib, who openly supported Gen Z 212 and called for the release of detainees.)

In activist circles, meanwhile, having a woman leading the government hasn’t been as important a subject of discussion as the struggle against corruption and the push for further democratization. At least some critics even see the discussion around Mansouri as a diversion from important political debates. Although they welcome a woman leader, leftists in the PSU and the Federation of the Democratic Left believe that structural political reform, social justice, and democratization are far more important than identity politics. Indeed, many Moroccan citizens seem more concerned about the reforms Mansouri will implement to ease the cost-of-living crisis than the gender dynamics at play.

Regardless, the royal nature of the decision leaves little room for open criticism. If Mansouri succeeds in overseeing reforms that improve both gender inequality and the socioeconomic climate, her premiership could have a considerable impact on Morocco’s evolution in the 21st century. At the same time, because she does not fully hold the reins of power, she could remain confined to a political role that critics view as an impediment to genuine democratic improvement. After all, if Morocco undergoes a meaningful transformation, it will be at the hands of the king, not Mansouri herself.

Ilhem Rachidi is a freelance reporter based in Morocco. She worked as a correspondent for four years at the French media site Mediapart and has written for Orient XXI, Rue89, Al-Monitor, and the Christian Science Monitor. X: @Ilhemrachidi

#6048. The petty joy of a blue election night

Ten years ago, watching the dawning of the Trump era on Fox News felt appropriate somehow. Notice that I didn’t say it felt right; after all, we were sinking into an anti-Enlightenment Age propped up by Rupert Murdoch’s propaganda machine. Nothing about any of that felt right.

Still, once the phrase “President-elect Donald Trump” became as inevitable as Thanos, and Fox’s anchors giggled like ascendant supervillains, staring into that snarling maw seemed like the responsible thing to do.

Training my focus on CNN and MS NOW in time to catch 2026’s predicted blue wave promised to be just as illuminating. Back in 2016, while everyone else on CNN struggled to make sense of what was happening, commentator Van Jones somberly characterized the results as “whitelash against a changing country.”

Shortly after Trump was inaugurated, he turned against CNN full force, branding it and every other outlet denying favorable coverage as fake news. Trump’s 2024 victory further endangered any media outlets outside of the right-wing echo chamber, as he hit news organizations with obscenely ridiculous legal complaints to force them to bend the knee.

So we’ll pardon Jones for his deliciously petty reaction to what Jake Tapper, the emcee of CNN’s “Election Night in America” telecast, awkwardly described as a “blue-nami.” By the time the Democrats took control of the House and Senate, the previously funereal Anderson Cooper was gleefully eager to hear what Jones had to say. And his colleague did not disappoint, delivering what may have been the night’s most satisfying monologue.

“If you join a cult, at some point the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-Aid,” he observed as chastened GOP pundit Scott Jennings sat inches away. “This is Jonestown for the Republican Party. They drank the Kool-Aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong . . .

“You join a cult, at some point, you go to Jonestown,” Jones repeated in closing. “That’s where you are tonight, Republicans.” Then he pretended to pass a cup to his Trumpian counterpart.

Election night news coverage is a stressful affair in the best of times. In 2026, CNN and MS NOW, the channel formerly known as MSNBC, entered the fray as battered underdogs. MS NOW is now owned by Versant, a group of cable channels spun off from NBCUniversal. CNN, part of Warner Bros. Discovery, will soon be owned by Skydance and its Trump-allied owner David Ellison.

Neither newsroom can claim relief over what’s on the horizon, which is why Cooper led CNN’s coverage with the air of an undertaker greeting democracy’s mourners. America’s major news outlets have been taking it on the chin with the rest of us — including Cooper, a former “60 Minutes” correspondent who fled Bari Weiss’ CBS takeover only for Ellison to come for his cable news shire anyway. Blue wave or not, CNN’s future is uncertain.

So although MS NOW may be scrappier and looser these days, at least its reporters and pundits aren’t working through an institutional existential crisis. That fatigue showed up in how CNN’s Magic Wall wrangler, John King, lived cautiously from moment to moment, allowing only a mild display of wonder as he shifted between the largely scarlet 2024 map and the much bluer 2026 version.

“What’s happening right now?” King wondered. “What’s the right word? Is it a rebuke? Is it repudiation? Is it shellacking? Is it a spanking? I mean, at the moment, this is the collapse of the president’s party on live television as you watch it play out.”

And for the first time in a decade of watching election nights, it was a joy to experience — like learning how to hope again.

Peddling optimism isn’t the job of any journalistic organization, of course. But knowing what CNN’s newsroom is contending with regardless of this election outcome makes their composure especially admirable. The CNN team had a 10-ton weight pressing down on them and still managed to convey the sense of celebration presumably gripping most of its viewers.

Most people tune out election night noise regardless of whether the vote goes in their favor, perhaps gleaning what they can from the flashy graphics and chyrons. This gave MS NOW’s Ali Velshi an advantage at the network’s Big Board now that his former co-worker Steve Kornacki has moved over to NBC. Both have earned fandoms by injecting levity into managing each election’s data flood.  On Tuesday night, Kornacki inspired a meme simply by being captured on his new network’s Kornacki Cam as he walked down a hall.

But Velshi kept his version of his predecessor’s two-step going, buzzing around on MS NOW’s Big Board with a hummingbird’s energy. “Annie Andrews is outperforming, and Darlene Graham is underperforming,” he rapidly blurted, breaking down the Democratic challenger’s road to her unexpected win in South Carolina over the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, before turning to the camera with a delightfully bemused look to say, “This is a totally weird conversation that we are having. Right?” It’s true. After years of polls overstating the Democrats’ chances, it did feel strange to have underestimated how much they’d win.

Still, Rachel Maddow‘s ebullience from the moment MS NOW’s coverage began was tough to beat. Before a single result came in, she cheerfully offered, “So far, the one thing we can definitively say is that Americans like our democracy, and they are enjoying using it in record numbers in this cycle.”

Once Democrats claimed majorities in the House and Senate a few hours later, she let loose. In calling the race for Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district for Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, Maddow couldn’t resist calling her Republican opponent, Rob Bresnahan, a “sometime ghost hunter” as her colleagues snickered in the background.

This is an understandable reaction to voters’ referendum on the president’s unpopular and economically detrimental policies. Americans, regardless of partisan stance, are struggling to afford the basics. But as Chris Hayes pointed to the shock of so many Democratic upsets, he noted that high prices aren’t the only thing forcing this drastic change. “The rot that is coming from the top of the country is very, very, very clearly on voters’ minds,” he said.

So if Jones wants to indulge in a little grave dancing, so be it.

It was even better to see other correspondents take stock of all the history made on Tuesday night. New Hampshire voters chose a Democrat, Chris Pappas, to join the U.S. Senate, making him the first out gay man elected to the chamber.

Voters turned Texas blue and elected four Black governors – including former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor in Georgia, and the first female Black governor in our country’s history.

Once that state’s contest for governor was called for Bottoms, MS NOW’s team tapped Symone Sanders-Townsend to contextualize what that meant for voters and Black women. Sanders-Townsend reminded us that when Trump calls Georgia to gripe, it will be Bottoms on the other end of the line. She’ll also be the one to ensure the 2028 election is certified for the rightful winner.

But when Sanders-Townsend’s colleagues asked her to share how Bottoms’ victory made her feel, her reaction hit home. “After the 2024 presidential election, for myself and Black women all over this country, it felt like a repudiation of us,” she said, holding back tears. “…There were Black women, myself included, that felt like, ‘Well, maybe America just does not want us.'”

So to Sanders-Townsend, and all the other Black women disappointed by their fellow citizens in 2024, Bottoms’ victory said, “Georgia wanted Keisha.”

That moment didn’t diminish Jones’ take on what this election night meant to him. “This is like Christmas and a birthday and an Easter bunny and Halloween!” he said. “This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy stand up.”

But by allowing herself to cry on camera, Sanders-Townsend broadcast a different kind of signal. She let us know that on this night, and for the first time in a long time, it was OK to ease into some sense of relief. And that’s better than the fleeting pleasure of retaliatory pettiness, well-earned though it may be.

#6046. Newsom’s death row commutations spark DA revolt; prosecutors warn of legal fight

Former DOJ prosecutor Jim Trusty reacts to Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute hundreds of death sentences, criticism from victims' families and questions about the decision's timing. He also weighs in on the federal investigations into Rep. Ilhan Omar's fraud allegations.

At least a dozen California district attorneys are publicly condemning Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute all 548 death sentences in the state, arguing the sweeping move overrides juries, disregards victims’ families and defies the will of state voters.

Newsom announced the plan Thursday, saying state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values. The move would convert the sentences to life without parole, though 382 cases still require approval from at least four California Supreme Court justices, according to The Associated Press.

In response, prosecuting attorneys across California have raised concerns about victims’ rights, the governor’s constitutional authority and the role of the California Supreme Court in reviewing hundreds of the commutations.

"Justice requires case-by-case consideration, not one-size-fits-all decisions," Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho said in response to Newsom's action.

THREE STATES CARRY OUT EXECUTIONS ON SAME DAY AMID RENEWED DEATH PENALTY DEBATE

A table fitted with restraints holds down death row prisoners while they are given a lethal injection at Huntsville Unit (Walls Unit) in Huntsville, Texas. (Greg Smith/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images)

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer described the move as "mercy for the wolves" that inflicts "the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep."

Spitzer noted that regulations implemented by California’s Board of Parole Hearings on Oct. 1 allow thousands of prisoners serving life without parole to become eligible for parole, arguing that Newsom's latest death row commutations could put these inmates "one step closer" to release. Newsom’s office says, however, that the affected prisoners will remain in prison and are not eligible for release.

"The governor is attempting to appear courageous with this decision. He is not courageous. His commutations are solely based upon power and political aspirations," added San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson, who accused Newsom of caring more about politics than people.

"Courage would require speaking with crime victims and the surviving family members of the people murdered by these death row inmates."

CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Anderson cited the case of Kevin Cooper, a California death row inmate convicted of killing Josh Ryen’s parents and sister and Ryen’s friend, Chris Hughes, and leaving Ryen for dead.

Anderson said Newsom did not contact Ryen or Hughes’ mother, Mary Ann Hughes, to ask their views on a possible commutation, and Ryen has never received a call from the governor.

"Courage would require the governor to follow Marsy’s Law, California’s constitutional rights belonging to victims of crime," Anderson continued. "He has not. I am not aware of any victims’ family members receiving notice of these commutations from the governor."

Anderson and several other California prosecutors who spoke out against Newsom's death row commutations also framed the dispute as a challenge to the jury system and an override of the will of California voters.

They said jurors in each case heard the evidence, weighed all the necessary factors and decided whether death was warranted, with judges and appellate courts later reviewing those verdicts. Newsom’s blanket action, they argue, substitutes one statewide decision for hundreds of individualized judgments.

NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson answers questions during a news conference outside the San Bernardino County Sheriff's Department in Rancho Cucamonga April 10, 2026. (Anjali Sharif-Paul, The Sun/SCNG)

"A single order commuting all of them would set aside hundreds of individualized judgments without examining the facts of even one," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow said.

"It invalidates the exhausting, emotionally wrenching work of our citizens who sat on juries, weighed horrific evidence and delivered lawful verdicts. Most unforgivably, it is a slap in the face to victims and their families," said San Joaquin District Attorney Ron Freitas.

"This decision does not bind wounds; it tears them wide open all over again."

The prosecutors pointed out that California voters rejected death penalty repeal initiatives in 2012 and 2016, while approving Proposition 66 in 2016, which changed procedures for challenging death sentences and was promoted by supporters as a way to speed up the process. The district attorneys argued Newsom’s blanket action overrides those ballot-box decisions without repealing the law.

"A blanket commutation is a mass erasure of justice. It overrides the will of California voters who have repeatedly defended capital punishment at the ballot box," Freitas added in his response to Newsom's action.

A prison is shown in an undated file photo as California district attorneys condemn Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute all 548 state death sentences. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Some California prosecutors who spoke out against Newsom's controversial move signaled that the dispute may not end with public statements.

San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan said her office was "researching any lawful remedies" that would allow victims’ voices to be heard and considered, while Kern County District Attorney Cynthia Zimmer was more direct, saying, "This assault on justice will be challenged."

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman acknowledged that commuting existing sentences falls within the governor’s constitutional authority, but said, "That power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty. Only the Legislature or the voters can do that."

Newsom’s clemency announcement clarifies that it "does not repeal the death penalty" and is limited to commuting California’s current death sentences.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

Barely 60 seconds into his 60 Minutes interview on Sunday—two days before the U.S. midterm election—Abdul El-Sayed was asked to pick the most important issue he was hearing about from voters in Michigan, where he ran for Senate.

“I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI,” El-Sayed said, listing a well-documented series of potential risks from artificial intelligence, including massive economic disruption to AI escaping human control. Barely 60 seconds into his 60 Minutes interview on Sunday—two days before the U.S. midterm election—Abdul El-Sayed was asked to pick the most important issue he was hearing about from voters in Michigan, where he ran for Senate.

“I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI,” El-Sayed said, listing a well-documented series of potential risks from artificial intelligence, including massive economic disruption to AI escaping human control. He laid out a list of proposals to mitigate those risks, including a “cabinet-level agency” to regulate AI, partial public ownership of AI companies, and “terms of engagement” for data centers that would be negotiated with local communities. He also advocated for a “full-on pause” on so-called frontier AI development, referring to the world’s most advanced models made by Silicon Valley giants such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft.

Come January, El-Sayed will have the opportunity to put that talk into action, having won one of the most high-profile races in the Democratic sweep of Congress. But he’s not the only Democratic candidate whose views on AI helped propel them to victory.

While the national blue wave is largely being seen as a repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump’s agenda, it also served as a referendum on AI and the data centers required to support them.

NBC exit polls found that 57 percent of voters believed that AI would do more harm to society than good, with 56 percent deeming the technology as “crucial or a major factor” in determining their vote. From Texas to Georgia to Ohio, voters opted to support candidates—mostly Democrats—who promised to rein in AI development and slow the data center buildout.

Strikingly, the Democratic blowout came despite Silicon Valley bigwigs—including Elon Musk, venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman along with his wife, Anna—spending more than half a billion dollars to back Republicans, who have widely been seen as less favorable to regulating AI over the past two years.

Many Republican candidates tried to backpedal their support for the unbridled AI development that Trump has advocated, but—as with many other issues—their association with the U.S. president appears to have outweighed those efforts in voters’ minds.

“I think this is the public doing the only thing it really can in the context of a governance regime in which there’s no real regulation in the United States,” Alondra Nelson, the former acting director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy under former President Joe Biden and the lead architect of the Biden administration’s Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, told Foreign Policy.

Nowhere is the opposition to AI more palpable than with data centers, whose numbers have exploded in the United States. These facilities, which house computing infrastructure, support the internet as we know it, underpinning everything from video streaming to web purchases. But the Trump administration’s push for AI dominance has led to the proliferation of bigger and more powerful facilities, including the “hyperscale” data centers used by tech giants.

More than 1,500 data centers are now being developed across the country, joining more than 3,000 facilities already in operation, according to the Pew Research Center. The boom has mostly centered on a handful of hot spots—namely Virginia, Texas, and California—although planned construction is now spreading to more regions.

Backlash has been fierce. From Maine to Utah, opposition has grown over the sheer pace of the buildout and the facilities’ impact on energy bills, water usage, jobs, land, and local pollution. Even before the midterms, polls suggested that more than two-thirds of Americans are against local construction of AI data centers, and at least 15 states have weighed moratoriums.

“You can’t fight against a Silicon Valley company, but you can fight against a data center being developed in your area,” said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin. “If that’s the only lever you have to pull, then that’s the lever you’re going to look to pull.”

And pull that lever they did. In Tuesday’s election, there were 41 local measures on the ballot across 10 states that would in some way restrict data center construction. In all but one of the cases, Americans voted against data centers, according to CNBC.

One of Democrats’ most stunning victories came in Texas, which has been a Republican stronghold for decades but has seen fierce debates play out over the state’s embrace of data centers. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott once courted data center investment in his pledge to make the state the “epicenter of AI development.” But so many data centers were built that they strained the state’s electrical grid, prompting public outrage. In June, Abbott told state regulators to make data centers bear the cost of the electrical infrastructure they need; in August, he ordered regulators to stop data center grid connections and directed audits.

Yet his late-stage pivot wasn’t enough to save him. On Tuesday, Abbott was unseated by Gina Hinojosa, who has urged an immediate moratorium on data center development. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, too, has called for stronger data center regulations. “Texas should be a leader when it comes to innovation and technology, but that only works if Texans get a say and get a share of that economic growth—and that’s not what’s happening right now,” he said in July.

Hinojosa’s call for a data center moratorium has been echoed by Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta who won the race to be Georgia’s governor.

In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated his Republican opponent, Jon Husted, despite millions in spending by tech billionaires to defeat Brown and support Husted’s campaign. Brown repeatedly criticized Husted as “the face of data centers” during his campaign. Democrat Annie Andrews also won the South Carolina Senate seat previously held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in another big upset—in part by dubbing her opponent, Graham’s sister, as “Data Center Darline.”

The techlash extended to the House, where two candidates in key races who centered AI safety issues—Manny Rutinel of Colorado and Scott Wiener of California—both won.

So what happens now? While there is broad recognition across the Democratic Party that AI regulation is needed, there is a wide range of proposals from current and prospective lawmakers on what form that regulation should take.

The midterm results could give more power to individual states to further their AI regulation and ensure more cohesion between the state and federal level. Trump administration orders to nationalize AI rulemaking have received significant Democratic congressional pushback over the past year, and New York, California, and Illinois have all put forward their own legislation to regulate AI. “What these three [states] share is that they are led by Democratic governors,” said Nelson. She suggested that we could now see regulations that states have piloted “being advanced at the federal level in a more accelerated way.”

Much of the immediate scrutiny and restrictions will likely target data centers, said Rhodes, given how much of a lightning rod they have become. “I imagine we’re still going to build a lot of data centers in this country,” he said, “but the scrutiny over cost allocation, water consumption, and community benefits are going to become real drivers in which projects get green lighted.” (Musk, who alone spent almost $450 million to help Republicans in the midterms, sardonically posted on X that “Data centers in space” were “looking pretty appealing right now.”)

But Ami Fields-Meyer, an author and political strategist who previously served as a senior policy advisor on AI and technology in the Biden administration, believes that voters are demanding action on far more than just data centers.

“It would be a big mistake for Democrats to misread these results as being only about data centers. This is about power and agency,” Fields-Meyer said. “After the [2008] financial crisis, we focused on providing immediate relief but failed to turn the rage the public felt at Wall Street into a broader reckoning,” he added. “But if congressional Democrats are smart, if they want to get the politics right, they won’t make that mistake again and they’ll see this as a much broader mandate to deal with corporate power in the tech industry.”

#6039. MAGA media scrambles to form a circular firing squad

Forty-five minutes before the first polls closed on Tuesday, Greg Gutfeld was still doing what Fox News does best, acknowledging reality just long enough to replace it with a culture-war hallucination. “Gas prices are so high, I’m going to vote for the party that wanted to trans my kids,” he joked on “The Five,” adding that he didn’t see Democratic wins on the horizon. “There is no blue wave materializing,” Clay Travis, the Outkick founder and Fox contributor, posted at 3 p.m. EST, adding that Republicans were surging in Florida and the polls were about to be proven wrong yet again.

Then the polls closed, and MAGA’s delusions were pulverized. The country that right-wing media had spent two years describing as angry, ascendant and permanently realigned voted in an avalanche that crushed years of manufactured MAGA hype. American voters told the president to take his $5,000 “Trump Dividend” checks and shove them. Elon Musk, who moved to Texas to get away from Democrats and then spent a reported $150 million to deliver the Lone Star State for Republicans, saw his early Tuesday post urging people to vote red disappear from his profile by Wednesday.

The country woke up to results that few expected — and a long list of historic firsts. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman governor in American history. Michigan sent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Washington as the first Muslim senator. New Hampshire elected Chris Pappas as the first openly gay man in the Senate. New Mexico made Deb Haaland the first Native American woman governor, and Peggy Flanagan became Minnesota’s first Native American woman senator. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa over three-term Gov. Greg Abbott — the state’s first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Ohio got its first woman governor in Dr. Amy Acton. South Carolina tapped Dr. Annie Andrews as its first elected woman senator. Democrats won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in 94 years. While votes are still being counted in key races, solid majorities in both the Senate and House are assured, and Democrats are set to make Hakeem Jeffries the country’s first Black speaker.

Even the New York Post, Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid and a loyal Trump house organ, refused to mince words on its front page: “Trump suffers historic rebuke as Dems romp in midterms,” with “BLUE TSUNAMI” blaring beneath it. On “Fox and Friends” Wednesday morning, Ainsley Earhart warned viewers that “your wallet and your way of life” are now in the crosshairs.

The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment.

It is no surprise that Trump 2.0, stripped of its previous establishment Republican guardrails like Mike Pence and Mitch McConnell, has culminated in such total structural collapse. The deeper truth the conservative media apparatus could never say out loud is that MAGA was always a Trump-specific phenomenon. It does not transfer to his imitators, and it only ever worked when the economy let voters treat Trump as entertainment. Right-wing media spent years confusing its ability to dominate a conversation with its ability to represent a country. When Tuesday’s returns exposed the difference, its leading voices reached for almost everything except accountability. They blamed immigration. They blamed insufficient restrictions on voting. They blamed each other. Alex Jones even decided Trump might secretly be a Democrat.

For the network’s election night coverage, Fox News seated former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio between two of Trump’s former press secretaries, Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt, and he told them to their faces that they were “missing the plot.” He said, “The American people are looking at a war they do not believe in, and they did not authorize. They’re looking at prices that are making it impossible for middle-class people, let alone working-class people, to live.”

Trump, watching at the White House, raged on Truth Social — “Why does FoxNews have deBlasio” — and seethed at the panel’s lone liberal: “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me.” After Gutfeld read the president’s text on air — which is as good a diagram as exists of what Fox News is now: a suggestion box the president monitors live — Tarlov answered on X, not on Truth Social: “Reality is a tricky thing,” and the president “should get better at dealing with it.”

On Newsmax, things were somehow worse. Political strategist Dick Morris argued that Trump’s problem was effectively excessive success: He had solved the major problems that would otherwise motivate Republican voters. The influencer ecosystem, meanwhile, went straight for the circular firing squad, and every faction picked a different target.

Jones, livestreaming as the returns buried his movement, said Trump himself is the plant: “I think he’s a Democrat. I’m 100% at war with Trump. He’s not that r*tarded. He did this on purpose. I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell and he works for them.” Benny Johnson and Libs of TikTok reached for the great replacement theory, and Fox’s Lawrence Jones supplied the broadcast version, surveying Texas and concluding, “Texas, there is a lesson here. Don’t be so welcoming.”

So much for celebrating people voting with their feet and the U-Hauls leaving California.

Laura Loomer went straight doomer: “America is over and so is the American Dream.” Others blamed Sen. John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE Act and shrink the electorate further, as though the answer to such a broad repudiation were fewer voters. The Daily Wire’s Ben Shapiro posted the “everything is fine” fire GIF — “Just checking in to see how things are goi—” — and the Federalist’s Sean Davis answered with the hot-dog-suit meme, the one where the man in the costume insists everyone else is the problem.

The recriminations got personal fast. Rep. Nancy Mace told Fox’s Mark Levin to “STFU,” blamed his “beloved” war for the losses and called the night “devastating . . . for the hard-working American who can’t afford to buy a home, or fill their tank with gas or put food on the table.” Levin returned fire: Mace was a “washed up political loser” and “one of the most mentally unhinged POS to ever be in Congress.” She was angry, he said, “because you’ll actually have to now work for a living . . . Good riddance, crackpot.” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis gloated that with governors’ races lost in Texas and Ohio and Georgia, the Sunshine State would stand alone among the ten most populous states with a Republican governor. And Katie Miller — podcaster, administration wife, professional MAGA explainer — told CBS’s Norah O’Donnell that she had not voted at all. “I did not vote in Virginia because in Virginia when you vote, you dox your own address, and so I prefer my own safety and security over giving that up.”

In the end, the movement’s loudest voices spent the cycle performing for each other. Some of them couldn’t even be bothered to vote.

#6036. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel’s Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

#6035. Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

In South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

Democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

In Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the new lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

After Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with new congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

With GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

Under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

Reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

Mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

The tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

And one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

Among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

#6034. Hoax Bomb Threats Disrupt Air Traffic Across Europe

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: Hoax Bomb Threats Disrupt Air Traffic Across Europe

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at hoax bomb threats targeting airlines in Europe, another national security conviction in Hong Kong, and the resignation of Paraguayan President Santiago Peña.

Hoax bomb threats targeted at least 27 different flights across Europe on Thursday, forcing planes to make unplanned landings or be escorted by fighter jets to their destinations. This was the second such incident to impact the continent this week, affecting thousands of travelers.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at hoax bomb threats targeting airlines in Europe, another national security conviction in Hong Kong, and the resignation of Paraguayan President Santiago Peña.

Hoax bomb threats targeted at least 27 different flights across Europe on Thursday, forcing planes to make unplanned landings or be escorted by fighter jets to their destinations. This was the second such incident to impact the continent this week, affecting thousands of travelers.

Although it is still unclear who is responsible for the massive air traffic disruption, several European officials and aviation experts suspect that Russia may be at least partly to blame.

Moscow has stepped up its hybrid warfare tactics on Ukraine and its European allies in recent months, from launching drone strikes to sabotaging critical infrastructure. That includes a failed drone attack on Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in August as well as repeated incursions into Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania.

“Russia remains aggressor No. 1,” Ken McCallum, the head of the United Kingdom’s internal security service, said last month in a speech highlighting the threat of Moscow’s hybrid warfare.

In many instances, though, NATO members have struggled to concretely prove that Russia is behind these attacks. “Identifying state sponsors of gray-zone acts is extremely difficult—by design,” FP columnist Elisabeth Braw argued in September, as these operations are often cheap to execute, easy to deny, and not expected to trigger armed retaliation.

This week’s bomb threats appear to have fallen into that category. Flights impacted included ones coming from or heading to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Spain, and the United Kingdom.

Many of those countries have also suffered recent cyberattacks on their supermarket refrigeration systems. Last month, hackers seized control of cooling systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spoiling food and sparking fires. And on Monday, hackers targeted fridges and freezers at dozens of stores in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Sweden.

This was a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it,” said Christophe Hansen, the European Union’s commissioner for agriculture and food.

Investigators have yet to determine who is behind the cyberattacks, and so far, there has been no established link between Monday’s supermarket hacks and this week’s airplane bomb threats. However, the back-to-back incidents have raised European authorities’ concerns about other potential vulnerabilities in the continent’s security.

10 years in prison. A Hong Kong court on Thursday sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison for collusion with foreign entities under the country’s national security law. Wong was convicted of working with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and other individuals to ask foreign governments to impose sanctions on China.

Wong, long considered one of the faces of Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement, was first detained in November 2020 after pleading guilty to inciting and organizing an unauthorized anti-government rally the previous year. “I have never advocated Hong Kong independence, nor have I ever promoted the ‘collapse of China’ or regime change,” Wong said ahead of Thursday’s sentencing, though he admitted to mistakenly believing that his actions abided by the law.

Nearly all of Hong Kong’s national security cases result in convictions, prompting many activists to plead guilty in the hopes of receiving a reduced sentence. In February, a Hong Kong court sentenced pro-democracy activist Jimmy Lai to 20 years in prison after he pleaded not guilty to similar charges.

Risk of impeachment. Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday in the face of a looming impeachment vote over the collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital moneylender that millions of residents use. “I do so with the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” ​Peña said.

On Monday, the Central Bank of Paraguay voted unanimously to seize Ueno after the company’s solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum; regulators argue that this was largely driven by massive insider loans. The seizure abruptly locked around 3 million customers (or roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adult population) out of their accounts, plunging the country into financial turmoil.

Lawmakers immediately took notice of Peña’s ties to Ueno, including his decision to remain a business partner of the conglomerate that owns the moneylender, and argued that the seizure was a conflict of interest. Legislators also accused Peña of institutional cover-ups and the misuse of pension funds. Peña and the bank have denied any wrongdoing.

Although Peña initially appeared ready to fight the allegations, the president quickly surrendered his post after ​Congress President Basilio Nuñez and Colorado Party President Horacio Cartes withdrew their support—making it all but certain that the impeachment vote would pass. Vice President Pedro Alliana will now take Peña’s place.

Diplomatic row. Tensions between Ethiopia and Sudan escalated on Wednesday, with both countries shuttering their consulates and expelling each other’s diplomats. The tit-for-tat moves were made in response to recent allegations that both governments are aiding rebel forces in each other’s territory.

On Friday, Sudan filed formal complaints to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union Peace and Security Council, accusing Ethiopia of providing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) with logistical support. Khartoum also claimed that Addis Ababa was hosting launching pads for RSF drone strikes on Sudanese electricity and fuel facilities. Ethiopia has denied supporting the RSF in Sudan’s deadly civil war.

Meanwhile, Ethiopia has accused Sudan of backing rebel forces fighting in its northern Tigray region, which has also suffered a devastating humanitarian crisis. Khartoum has similarly rejected allegations that it has aided armed groups in Tigray.

The accusations and diplomatic expulsions risk pulling Ethiopia and Sudan into a more direct conflict. “The Sudanese government remains committed to its right to defend its territory. Nevertheless, it is making ⁠every possible effort to avoid an open war with Ethiopia,” said Amjad Farid, a senior advisor for Sudan’s Transitional Sovereign Council.

Star soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday that he is retiring from playing for Portugal, ending a 23-year international career defined by record-setting games and intense rivalries. “The day has come back for me to hand back the number 7 shirt of our national team,” Ronaldo said in a video on social media. With the men’s soccer record of 234 international appearances and 146 goals for Portugal, Ronaldo is largely seen as one of the greatest soccer players of all time. He will continue to play as a forward for al-Nassr in the Saudi Pro League, in a move that has drawn allegations of sportswashing for Riyadh’s poor human rights record.

Trump wore a Dalma suede bomber jacket by Nour Hammour, paired with an Adam Lippes skirt and Manolo Blahnik BB pumps for the occasion, blending her signature polished style with a more relaxed look suited to a college football weekend.

LSU cheerleaders flanked Trump during her remarks, and the Tiger mascot presented her with both scholarship checks while wearing a signature "Be Best" T-shirt.

First lady Melania Trump arrives at Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport on Saturday in Baton Rouge, La., en route to Louisiana State University to an event announcing scholarships for LSU students who came through the foster care system as part of her "Fostering the Future" program. First lady Melania Trump attends an event to announce a $5 million Fostering the Future Endowment Fund at Louisiana State University, Saturday, in Baton Rouge. (Annabelle Gordon/Pool/Getty Images)

"At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere, but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said.

First lady Melania Trump stands with scholarship recipients at LSU as part of her "Fostering the Future" program. (Fox News Digital/Jasmine Baehr)

She closed with an encouraging message to scholarship recipients.

"To the Fostering the Future scholars here today, and throughout America: I see you. I believe in you. And I will keep working to create new opportunities with you," she said.
