#6030. At the Races: After the deluge

By Mary Ellen McIntire, Daniela Altimari and Niels Lesniewski

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they’ve so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That’s how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6029. New Jersey town reveals staggering $26M theft days after election, sparking backlash

Residents of a New Jersey township are demanding answers after officials revealed a $26 million fraudulent wire transfer more than five weeks after the theft, just days after a local election.

A New Jersey township is facing backlash after officials revealed that $26 million was stolen in a fraudulent wire transfer, with residents questioning why the massive theft wasn't disclosed until more than five weeks later — just days after Election Day.

Cranbury Township Mayor Lisa Knierim announced Friday that the municipality had been the victim of a "sophisticated financial theft" involving approximately $26 million.

Knierim, a Democrat, said the fraudulent wire transfer took place on Sept. 28, with the funds originally designated for purchasing property to meet the township's affordable housing obligations.

A task force involving local, county, state and federal law enforcement agencies, led by the township's police department and the Middlesex County Prosecutor's Office, is working to recover the funds, according to the mayor's statement.

CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY

Cranbury Township officials disclosed a $26 million fraudulent wire transfer on Nov. 6, more than five weeks after the theft occurred and three days after Election Day. (Google Maps)

So far, investigators have frozen nearly $17.3 million in assets, leaving approximately $8.7 million outside the reported freeze.

The township said the investigation remains active, adding that additional details cannot be released.

Knierim's announcement came Nov. 6, three days after the midterm elections and more than five weeks after the theft.

Several residents responded to the announcement on the township's Facebook page, questioning the timing of the disclosure and demanding greater transparency from local officials.

NEW JERSEY MAYOR WHO CHARGED AT RESIDENT DURING COUNCIL MEETING CONCEDES ELECTION LOSS

Democrats retained control of the Cranbury Township Committee following an election held three days before officials publicly disclosed a $26 million financial theft. (Kena Betancur/Getty Images)

"I'm interested in knowing why this information was kept under wraps until after Election Day," one commenter wrote.

Another asked, "If this occurred on September 28th why is it just now being shared?"

The announcement followed Tuesday's local election, in which Democrat Thomas Szczur Jr. defeated Republican Carol Haring with 63.69% of the vote to Haring's 36.32%, according to election results published by the New Jersey secretary of state's office.

Szczur's victory preserved Democrats' control of all five seats on the Cranbury Township Committee.

The mayor acknowledged residents' concerns in her statement.

"We recognize that news of this magnitude will understandably raise questions and concerns among our residents," Knierim wrote. "Those concerns are legitimate, and we take them seriously."

NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS

A New Jersey township is facing questions from residents after officials revealed that approximately $26 million intended for affordable housing-related property purchases had been stolen. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Knierim also said the township was taking steps to strengthen financial oversight and maintain municipal operations, noting that the Township Committee plans to introduce ordinances Monday to establish two new positions: assistant township administrator and assistant chief financial officer.

The committee also plans to consider hiring a municipal accounting firm for additional financial consulting support, while officials work with insurance carriers to explore potential recovery options.

It remains unclear why the township waited more than five weeks to publicly disclose the theft.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the mayor's office for additional comment.

#6027. U.S. Foes React to the GOP’s Midterm Wipeout

Situation Report: U.S. Foes React to the GOP’s Midterm Wipeout

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report, where we’re back at full strength after our vacations to unpack the seismic U.S. midterm election results.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: U.S. foes react to the GOP’s midterm wipeout, Ukrainians express hope over the results, and how Democrats plan to challenge Trump’s foreign policy in a new Congress.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report, where we’re back at full strength after our vacations to unpack the seismic U.S. midterm election results.

Here’s what’s on tap for the day: U.S. foes react to the GOP’s midterm wipeout, Ukrainians express hope over the results, and how Democrats plan to challenge Trump’s foreign policy in a new Congress.

Top U.S. adversaries are trying to read the tea leaves on what the Republican Party’s shellacking in the 2026 midterms means for U.S. President Donald Trump’s foreign policy moving forward.

Starting in January, congressional Democrats will have powerful tools to constrain Trump—and they’ve pledged to challenge him on issues ranging from the Iran war to Ukraine. But the U.S. president will still have immense authority over foreign-policy and national security decisions.

Along these lines, here’s how Iran, Russia, and China are interpreting the results so far.

Tehran gloats. Iran framed the historic GOP defeat as American voters rejecting Trump’s war against the country. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote in a post on X.

He’s right. As even U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance noted, the Iran war’s economic impact played a significant role in turning voters against Republicans nationwide.

Yet Tehran also doesn’t appear to anticipate any major shifts in U.S. policy toward Iran despite the fact that Democrats will soon control Congress. “If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they’re gravely mistaken,,” Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei wrote in a post on X.

Though the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iran in the days leading up to the midterms, Trump had pledged no major escalation until after the vote. International mediators such as Qatar have recently sought to rekindle diplomatic discussions between Tehran and Washington in the hope of reaching a deal and preventing another round of heavy fighting. Trump is now pondering his legacy, and it’s still unclear whether he’ll move to cut his losses and end the war or try to save face with a fresh military operation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also facing a possible loss of power following national elections in his country, has reportedly been pressing Trump to return to war. But a majority of Americans now view the Israeli government unfavorably, and there’s growing bipartisan support for reassessing Washington’s ties with the country—all of which could factor into Trump’s next move regarding Iran.

An optimistic Kremlin. The midterms took place amid renewed efforts by the Trump administration to push for a Ukraine-Russia peace deal. The United States is poised to mediate talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.

Trump has faced bipartisan criticism in Washington for his handling of this process, as the president has once again soured on continued support for Kyiv while moving to reduce financial constraints on Moscow. Though a Democratic-led Congress is poised to push for stronger U.S. backing for Ukraine, the Kremlin appears hopeful that Trump will continue with his recent approach to peace negotiations and relations with Russia.

“President Trump remains in office. We sincerely hope that he will continue his peacemaking efforts. There is already some groundwork in place. Another round of trilateral talks is coming up very soon. These include successful peacemaking and humanitarian initiatives. We hope that all of this will continue. Ultimately, this is an internal American matter,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told a Russian journalist regarding the midterm results.

China shrugs. Washington’s biggest economic and military rival is doing little to reveal its true feelings about the midterm power shift ahead of a prospective meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen later this month. Asked about the election results on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, Chinese foreign ministry spokespersons Mao Ning and Guo Jiakun had identical answers: “The U.S. midterm elections are a domestic affair. China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state, enhance communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity.”

Even the opinion page of the state-run Global Times newspaper, usually a reliable source of hot takes on U.S. politics and policy, has been conspicuously silent on the midterms save for one editorial that took a gratuitous swipe at Europe.

Trump’s desire for a meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un could also be impacted by the U.S. leader’s diminished political standing. North Korea conducted yet another series of missile tests the day after the midterms and appears uninterested in a possible meeting in Shenzhen between Trump and Kim, with Kim’s sister Kim Yo Jong slamming the United States as “hostile” and “unreasonable” in a statement on Wednesday and adding that North Korea had “no need to sit face-to-face” with Trump.

The midterm results—and the major role that the Iran war played in the election—have raised questions over whether Trump will move to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Recent reports have suggested that Trump is asking political allies about this and considering making Hegseth the fall guy for failures in the war. Publicly, though, Trump continues to stand behind the Pentagon chief.

“I have every intention to keep him,” Trump said of Hegseth on Thursday. But the president also said he’s been receiving calls from people who are unhappy with Hegseth and doesn’t “understand why.”

But there are growing signs that Hegseth could soon face a House impeachment vote.

Meanwhile, former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who stepped down in September—reportedly over disagreements with Hegseth—has joined the tech giant OpenAI as senior counselor for national security modernization.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Ukraine’s cautious optimism. FP’s Sam Skove is reporting on the ground in Ukraine right now, where he spoke with Ukrainians about the U.S. midterm results. They expressed hope that Kyiv will receive more support from the United States with Democrats in control of Congress—but with winter on the horizon, they also have larger concerns closer to home. Read the full piece from Sam and FP’s Christina Lu here.

Democrats’ next moves. When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, it won’t just be the Iran war that Democrats want to take action on. FP’s staff wrote a breakdown of the top foreign-policy priorities for Democrats after the midterms. Read it here.

Riot police stand guard in front of the National Congress of Paraguay during an extraordinary session to decide on the possible impeachment of President Santiago Peña in Asunción on Nov. 5. Peña resigned on Thursday. Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images

Monday, Nov. 9: The U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) begins in Turkey.

The U.S. House and Senate reconvene for the first time since the midterm elections.

Tuesday, Nov. 10: Ukraine, Russia, and the United States are scheduled to conduct trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi.

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Deadline for Israeli President Isaac Herzog to nominate a candidate to form the next government.

41—the number of local ballot measures seeking restrictions on data centers in the midterm elections. All but one of them passed, as Rishi and Christina reported.

“J.D. Habibi. There is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.”

—Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed with a dig at Vance in his victory speech on Tuesday.

#6026. Taika Waititi’s Instagram crash out is a Trumpian sore loss

For all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world â and there are so, so many â heâs also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal governmentâs medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if weâre not careful, weâre all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, âKlara and the Sun.â After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the filmâs distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movieâs wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedyâs reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

Waititiâs childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isnât akin to Donald Trumpâs most damning sins, Waititiâs mockery is a symptom of a problem that wonât be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that âKlara and the Sunâ was âreboundingâ with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the filmâs 25% critics score. (For what itâs worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a filmâs quality.) âI havenât read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,â Waititi captioned the post. âBut I do listen to the people . . . Letâs spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldnât achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.â

Reading Waititiâs emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trumpâs favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a âSAD!â at the end of Waititiâs caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trumpâs poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, âThe critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.â)

Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititiâs caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trumpâs agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesdayâs midterms. But judging by the results, MAGAâs influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended â at least for now.

Not to be all, âOh, wonât someone think of the celebrities?â about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that itâs bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isnât akin to Trumpâs most damning sins, Waititiâs mockery is a symptom of a problem that wonât be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, âJojo Rabbit,â which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propagandaâs influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititiâs writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: Itâs downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics â people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi â just six years later.

But this is the rot that social media creates. Whether itâs Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.Â

For some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the monthâs salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today â to pursue oneâs passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one â is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesnât stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, itâs that things arenât just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

What Waititi fails to realize is that heâs not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But thatâs hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social mediaâs effect on human behavior, itâs had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyoneâs a critic, then no one is, and thatâs precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like theyâre poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

But itâs not just Waititi whoâs vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether itâs a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer techâs sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. Iâve seen this affect criticsâ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

Whatâs most concerning in Waititiâs response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before itâs even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other peopleâs perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion shows maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger wonât do anything for a personâs growth, artistic or otherwise. Americaâs politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

If Americaâs blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerbergâs Instagram, we owe some props to one of the centuryâs most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkinâs âThe Social Reckoningâ actually got a few things right. In last monthâs companion piece to âThe Social Network,â Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his directorâs eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. âIâm worried that the parts of directing that Iâm not good at are those parts you canât learn,â he admitted.

While there may be truth to his concern, Sorkinâs introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, itâs that things arenât just good because one person says so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

#6024. Inside a rancher family's clash with gov't that could have ripple effect right to SCOTUS: ‘Existential threat’

King Ranch owners Wade and Teresa King and Pacific Legal Foundation senior attorney Oliver Dunford discuss their fight with the Washington State Department of Ecology over a $267,540 fine and their push for a jury trial.

The owners of a multigenerational cattle ranch say they are facing an "existential threat" after the Washington state Department of Ecology fined them hundreds of thousands of dollars over their stockwater ponds, and they are warning the case could have substantial implications nationwide.

The department fined Wade and Teresa King, owners of King Ranch in Grant and Douglas counties, $267,540 in 2023 for allegedly damaging regulated wetlands by digging ponds to provide water for their ranching operations. The Kings argue the areas, which they were ordered to restore, are long-standing stockwater ponds for their livestock, not regulated wetlands.

The Kings, who have been trying to get their case in front of a jury, told Fox News Digital that, not only is their financial stability at stake, so are the rights of other ranchers.

"Losing this fight would be an existential threat," Wade said. "I don't know how we would recover from that, to be honest with you."

King Ranch owners Wade and Teresa King are fighting the Washington state Department of Ecology over areas the state says are regulated wetlands. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)

When the Kings were first hit with the fines and restoration orders, they immediately set out to challenge them. However, the department's required process directed them to bring their case before the Pollution Control Hearings Board (PCHB), an administrative panel that does not provide jury trials.

In March, the Kings filed a separate lawsuit in Grant County Superior Court, arguing the case should not be decided by the PCHB and that doing so would violate their right to a jury trial. Months later, a judge dismissed the lawsuit, ruling the Kings first had to complete the administrative process.

The Kings appealed the decision, and a Washington Court of Appeals commissioner paused the PCHB proceedings in September while the court considers whether they are entitled to a jury trial.

"It's all under the executive branch, and they very rarely go with the property owner," Wade said, adding that Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, who was attorney general when the fight began, now has appointment authority over the board alongside the state Senate.

"They almost always side with the agencies and it's just not a fair trial for appellants like us."

The PCHB declined to comment due to the pending case.

Oliver Dunford, a senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation representing the Kings, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to petition the U.S. Supreme Court if they are unsuccessful in Washington.

HOW A SIX PACK OF BEER AND THE MAGNA CARTA COULD FINALLY FIX A PROBLEM PLAGUING AMERICANS FOR DECADES

The Kings were fined $267,540 in 2023 for allegedly damaging regulated wetlands by digging cattle ponds. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)

"We have to ask them one question: to rule that the Seventh Amendment does apply against the states, and then to argue that the Kings should have had a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment," Dunford said.

He said if the case reaches the Supreme Court, a ruling could have ripple effects across other states.

"If we prevail, it would have an enormous effect, certainly across the state of Washington, but hopefully across the country, and prevent these agencies from just issuing these fines and then essentially putting the burden on you to prove your innocence and take the case all the way to the Supreme Court just to get a chance at a jury trial," he said.

The Kings' attorneys estimate the cost of complying with the department's orders could exceed $3.7 million. But beyond the financial toll, Teresa said the orders would be "unachievable" because the areas were never wetlands in the first place.

BLUE STATE'S WATER FAILURES COULD THREATEN FOOD SUPPLIES ACROSS US, LAWMAKER WARNS

The Kings argue the areas are stockwater ponds and are fighting to have their case heard by a jury. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)

"How do we as ranchers turn these into wetlands and comply with everything that Ecology wants us to?" she said. "It'll be unachievable and it would just spin us in the ground financially."

"How are we supposed to make wetlands from non-wetlands?" Wade added.

Wade said the department has failed to give them any details on how to fix the alleged damage. He said the wetlands designation gives the department greater authority over the areas than it would if they were considered stockwater ponds.

"That's the big reason why they want to call them wetlands when they're not wetlands," Wade said.

Wade and Teresa described how the fight could also hurt their children and their children’s children. The Kings have ranched in Grant and Douglas counties since the 1950s, where Teresa said multiple generations now live and work.

TRUMP ADMIN SCRAPS ‘WEAPONIZED’ WILDLIFE RULE THAT BECAME 'BURDEN' ON AMERICAN FAMILIES AND BUSINESSES: BURGUM

The Kings say the legal battle could affect other ranchers and their constitutional rights. (Wade and Teresa King/Pacific Legal Foundation)

"It’s fourth generation, then we have fifth and sixth living and working on this ranch, and we want to continue with this," she said. "We just want to be left alone."

The department said its investigation found no evidence the areas were previously stockwater ponds and accused the Kings of "damaging 23 naturally occurring wetlands" in Grant County.

"Ecology inspectors made site visits to these damaged areas where possible, but also used satellite imagery, aerial images dating from as far back as 1949, and other records to determine that the Kings had damaged 6.37 acres of naturally occurring wetlands by excavating, recontouring, and putting fill in them," the department said.

The department added it "repeatedly sought to resolve concerns about the damage" but the Kings "refused to cooperate with these efforts." They said they ordered the Kings to restore 11 more areas in Douglas County last year, bringing the total to 34, and most were on state land.

Wade said they have always protected and cared for the land that the department is now accusing them of damaging.

"We want clean water," Wade said. "Why would we pollute or cause damage to the land or the water that we rely on in our livelihood? We're generational. Why would we do something to harm ourselves that way and harm the environment?"

The Kings said the fight is far from over, with Teresa arguing the case could jeopardize exemptions other ranchers rely on to provide water for livestock.

"It's not just us," Teresa said. "We are defending every rancher in the state of Washington's exempt livestock water rights."

Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

#6023. How Foreign Policy Shaped These 3 Critical Midterm Races

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: How Foreign Policy Shaped These 3 Critical Midterm Races

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Republicans’ historic defeat in the U.S. midterms made clear that voters are unhappy with President Donald Trump’s Iran war quagmire and high tariffs, both of which are blamed for worsening the affordability crisis.

Beneath those top-line takeaways, however, there are other lessons to be learned. Three races in particular offer vital insight into how American voters view key planks of Trump’s global agenda—from Israel to tariffs to immigration—and what that could mean for the future of U.S. foreign policy.

Republicans’ historic defeat in the U.S. midterms made clear that voters are unhappy with President Donald Trump’s Iran war quagmire and high tariffs, both of which are blamed for worsening the affordability crisis.

Beneath those top-line takeaways, however, there are other lessons to be learned. Three races in particular offer vital insight into how American voters view key planks of Trump’s global agenda—from Israel to tariffs to immigration—and what that could mean for the future of U.S. foreign policy.

Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed bested former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race, where Israel took center stage throughout the campaign.

El-Sayed has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza and apartheid in the West Bank. He wants unconditional U.S. military support to end for not only Israel but also other Middle Eastern countries such as Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

This summer, El-Sayed narrowly defeated establishment Democrats’ preferred candidate in Michigan—moderate Rep. Haley Stevens—in a primary contest where U.S. policy toward Israel was the major dividing issue. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent at least $30 million to boost Stevens in the primary and then spent millions more trying to help Rogers in the general election.

By winning the race, El-Sayed showed that strong opposition to U.S. support for Israel is not only no longer a political third rail, but also that it can even be part of a successful campaign message. His victory demonstrates just how radically formerly staunch U.S. support for Israel has soured among not only liberals and progressives but also even with some Republican voters.

U.S. attitudes toward Israel have been colored by the country’s brutal war in Gaza as well as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s perceived role in convincing Trump to launch the Iran war in February. Among Democrats, Israel’s favorability rating out of a score of a possible 100 has slipped from 52 in 2022 to just 30 today, according to an October opinion survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs. And among Republicans, favorable views have fallen from 69 to 62 points.

Now, even Republicans seem to be waking up to the vibe shift. Trump abruptly claimed on Tuesday that nearly $4 billion in annual U.S. security assistance to Israel would end this year. “The left uses the $4 billion payment—that everybody knows about, it’s no secret—as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen,” Trump said in making the announcement.

And on Wednesday, U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance listed “change our relationship to Israel” as one of the four major policy adjustments that Republicans should make to win back voters who chose Trump in 2024 based on messaging from pollsters he spoke with.

From the Iran war to boat strikes to Ukraine, Democrats now have powerful leverage.

Trump’s tariffs are unpopular, and lawmakers want to claw back their authority.

The trade war that Trump instigated with Ottawa in 2025 has been felt across the United States, but especially in the northern states where the lengthy border with Canada has long been seen as an opportunity for integrating local economies, especially in the energy and automotive sectors.

Canada designed its retaliatory tariffs for massive political impact, targeting states that are heavily reliant on exports to Canada and had competitive midterms. In Michigan, exports to Canada fell by about $3.5 billion from 2024-2025 while the state lost more than 15,600 jobs, according to the Globe and Mail. And Canadian imports to Maine decreased by 8 percent from January 2025 to this August.

Republicans have largely backed Trump’s shifting explanations for why he was imposing steep tariffs on Canadian exports, including aluminum, steel, timber, and copper. Former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu, who unsuccessfully attempted on Tuesday to flip the New Hampshire Senate seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, was among them.

Early on, Sununu defended Trump’s tariffs on Canada and other countries. “If they want access to the American market, they’re going to have to either change those nontariff barriers or face some form of tariff. I think that message is an important one,” he said in an October 2025 interview at the start of his Senate campaign.

But as New Hampshire’s businesses suffered from retaliatory Canadian tariffs (the country is the state’s second-largest export market), Sununu eventually changed his tune. Retaliatory tariffs are estimated to have cost New Hampshire $1.1 billion since January 2025, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation.

In an October debate with his rival, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, Sununu acknowledged that the trade war with Canada was a “huge mistake” and said that he hadn’t meant to minimize the economic impact of the tariffs on New Hampshire’s businesses and consumers.

Yet it was apparently too little, too late. Pappas made hay over Sununu’s shifting stance on Trump’s tariffs, drawing attention to his own legislation in Congress that would exempt small businesses from tariffs on Canadian goods.

Pappas soundly defeated Sununu by a nearly 14-point margin.

“We’re in a big hole right now, and I’m hoping the Democrats, everything that they said, that they’re going to work for better for us, for prices of food—everything, gas, whatever it takes,” a New Hampshire voter named Donna said in a local television interview.

Latino voters helped drive Trump’s return to power in 2024. He received 42 percent of the national Latino vote that year, a record for any Republican presidential candidate. But after nearly two years of his sweeping mass deportation agenda, as well as trade and war policies that worsened an affordability crisis felt heavily by Latino voters, many of them appear to have turned against the U.S. president.

That was evident Tuesday in a district in Miami-Dade County in South Florida that is more than 70 percent Latino. At time of writing, three-term Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar was barely hanging on to the lead in her race, which could head to a recount. In contrast, Trump carried her district by 15 points in the 2024 presidential contest.

The district comprises an interesting grouping of Latino voters—including many whose families fled communist Cuba and who support Trump’s efforts to economically squeeze Havana so hard that the regime capitulates to U.S. demands or topples over. It also has a large population of Venezuelan Americans who fled the authoritarian regime of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and who credit Trump for capturing and arresting Maduro in a January military raid.

Yet for many Latino voters in the district, those welcome policy moves were overshadowed by the fear and economic disruption caused by Trump’s aggressive immigration and deportation strategy.

An October survey of Cuban Americans by Florida International University found that 61 percent backed continuing the U.S. embargo on trade with Cuba, but 76 percent disapproved of Trump’s deportation of Cuban nationals without a criminal record; 48 percent disapproved of his handling of the U.S. economy.

Evidently sensing the electoral peril that she was in, Salazar in September released an ad in which she addressed Trump, telling him that “some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.” Though she was criticized by the MAGA wing of the Republican Party, her campaign efforts to triangulate her positions on immigration with support for Trump may well save her seat.

But the warnings for Republicans on falling support with Latino voters are clear. Republicans largely rested their redistricting efforts in Florida on the assumption that Trump would be able to maintain his 2024 share of Latino and other nonwhite voter support. That assumption proved false on Tuesday, with Democrats winning three heavily Latino Florida House seats that Republicans had redrawn.

“The voters have spoken loud and clear all over District 27, Florida, and the rest of the country, that my party—my Republican Party—needs to course-correct on the economy and on immigration,” Salazar told supporters on election night.

Rachel Oswald is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @OswaldRachel

#6022. The grocery store shortcuts that make weeknight dinners easier

A version of this recipe first appeared in The Bite, Salon's food newsletter. Sign up for early access to articles like this, plus recipes, food-related pop culture recommendations and conversations about what we're eating, how and why.

There is a particular little sequence to my autumn evenings that Iâve come to adore.

I finish work, head to a dance class or the gym, and come home ready to cook. I pour myself a little cooking-time spritz â my current favorite is ginger-flavored sparkling water mixed with iced green tea and a squeeze of lemon â put on an old sitcom Halloween episode and open the refrigerator to see what weâre working with.

I love this part of the day. I love gathering ingredients, turning on the stove, deciding what sounds good. I especially love sitting down to something delicious afterward, knowing Iâve fed the muscles I just worked.

What I donât particularly love? Dirtying three separate bowls to bread chicken cutlets on a Tuesday night. Or peeling and chopping a pile of vegetables when Iâm already hungry. Or washing an enormous stack of dishes by hand, which has become an especially relevant consideration since my dishwasher gave up the ghost over the summer (and its replacement is currently in apartment maintenance limbo).Â

Which brings me to one of my more firmly held beliefs about home cooking: We canât be domestic goddesses for everything, you know?

And over the past several months, Iâve received a handful of emails from readers asking what packaged, prepared and otherwise convenient foods I actually buy. As it turns out, I have surprisingly strong opinions about groceries.

So, a little disclosure before we get into it: Nobody is paying me to recommend these products, and neither Salon nor I will earn money from these recommendations. These are simply the things I buy, use and genuinely enjoy. Some are specific brands; others Iâll happily buy from whichever label happens to be on sale.

For me, eating well right now means a dinner that takes less than an hour, includes at least two vegetables and some protein, ideally gives me a little more fiber, doesnât leave the kitchen looking like a crime scene and, above all, tastes really, really good.

And if spending a little extra on a convenience ingredient keeps me from placing an impulsive takeout order? Well, thatâs a pretty good investment, too.

Hereâs whatâs earning its keep in my kitchen lately.

Whole Foods frozen fried garlic breaded chicken breast fillets: I cannot overstate my affection for these things. Frankly, theyâre better than the breaded cutlets I usually make myself, and they eliminate the entire flour-egg-breadcrumb production, along with its accompanying dishes. Iâll serve them over pasta and vegetables, chop them into Caesar wraps or turn them into absolutely gorgeous fried chicken sandwiches. A box in the freezer is several possible dinners.

Frozen miniature meatballs: Any brand, really! I love these little guys for their versatility. For a quick stroganoff-ish dinner, Iâll simmer them with mushrooms, frozen aromatics, a gravy packet and fresh thyme, then finish everything with sour cream. Spoon the result over egg noodles, mashed potatoes or rice. Theyâre also excellent browned and added to Mediterranean-inspired bowls with rice, lemon hummus, feta, olives and a chopped cucumber-tomato salad. And when I want something comforting, Iâll toss them into pastina with finely diced vegetables for what I think of as âtiny everything soup.â

Heyday Canning Saucy Beans: Oh, how I love these. The beans come swimming in almost velvety sauces that are good enough that Iâd aspire to make them myself. The cans suggest simply heating and eating, which I wholeheartedly endorse. In fact, Iâve been known to sneak a cold bite of the tomato alla vodka beans straight from the can. No regrets. That variety is especially good as the foundation for a cozy skillet dinner, while the enchilada-flavored beans are excellent warmed and spooned over a rice bowl.

Laoban Popcorn Chicken with Soy Garlic Sauce: This freezer find really does scratch the takeout itch. The chicken pieces cook up light and crisp, while the sauce is a little bit of sticky heaven. I love serving them over rice with whatever vegetables I have waiting in the freezer, perhaps some steamed edamame, corn and shredded cabbage.

Jennyâs Tofu Organic Smoked Five Spice Tofu: Jennyâs tofu is made about 10 minutes from my Chicago apartment, and interviewing Jenny herself a few years ago helped convince me that many people who think they dislike tofu have simply never had really good, fresh tofu. The smoked variety is particularly wonderful for sandwiches. I love a barbecue smoked-tofu wrap with shredded red cabbage and corn relish, or a bÃ¡nh mÃ¬-inspired sandwich with crunchy vegetables.

Frozen scallion pancakes: Again, Iâm not especially brand-loyal. I like to treat these almost like tostadas, crisping them up and piling them high with toppings. One favorite is a sesame-scented chicken salad made with Kewpie mayonnaise, plenty of scallions and a little sesame oil. Spoon that over a hot scallion pancake for a delightful contrast of crisp, creamy and savory.

I once heard a piece of advice about eating more vegetables that Iâve never forgotten, although I wish I could remember who said it: Find the vegetables you can add to a meal almost automatically. The ones that make you say, âWhy the hell not?â

For me, those are pre-shredded cabbage and carrots.

Pre-shredded red and green cabbage: I put this on practically everything. Tacos, rice bowls, steak chili, prepared grain salads â anything that could benefit from a little crunch, color or freshness. I also love tossing green cabbage with miso butter, roasting it until the edges begin to brown, and finishing it with lemony, toasted panko breadcrumbs. Itâs inexpensive, keeps beautifully in the refrigerator and requires very little effort to turn into something special.

Pre-shredded carrots: These get tossed into stew bases, pasta sauces and curries, particularly anything Iâm planning to blend. Theyâre also the foundation of my current obsession: hibachi-style carrot-ginger dressing, which becomes almost laughably easy when you use frozen ginger and onion cubes, too.

Then thereâs my increasingly substantial frozen vegetable collection.

Fire-roasted corn, peas and carrots, mixed vegetables, edamame, spinach and cubed butternut squash: These are all regulars in my freezer. A note: Frozen vegetables are best with a little love. Iâll make compound butter to toss with them before roasting, whip up a herby sauce to coat them after steaming or finish them with a drizzle of brown butter, which is, in my opinion, king of nearly everything.

Iâve also become a fan of using prepared specialty cheese spreads to make indulgent broccoli. Break the florets â fresh or frozen â into small pieces, coat them with a good cheese spread (smoked Gouda and whipped Asiago have both been winners), and bake until bubbly, adding breadcrumbs if you like.

The philosophy is pretty simple: Iâd rather spend my energy making vegetables taste wonderful than spend all that time chopping them.

Now, hereâs where Iâm willing to get a little spendy.

I will not pay a premium for a bag of frozen vegetables that Iâm going to zhush up anyway. Generic peas are perfectly fine by me.

But sauces, pastes, condiments, good jams? Thatâs another story.

Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto: One of my current favorites. Itâs creamy, acidic and provides a really distinct little lift to almost anything I spoon it over. I love tossing it with cubetti pasta, peas and canned white beans for a quick pasta salad, but itâs also fantastic smeared on sourdough toast and piled with olive oil-marinated vegetables.

Sun-dried tomato pesto: Another little jar of concentrated goodness. I love its deep, savory tomato flavor in pasta, sandwiches and vegetables. It also happens to be a key player in one of my favorite semi-homemade chicken sandwiches, which weâll get to shortly.

Curry paste: A good curry paste is an invitation to improvise. Add protein, vegetables, some coconut milk or stock, and youâre already well on your way to something fragrant and satisfying.

Mekhala Lemongrass Turmeric Paste: Just this week, I stirred a spoonful into a soup base of frozen onions, garlic and ginger, then added coconut cream, frozen mushrooms, shredded carrots, leftover rice and shredded rotisserie chicken. I finished the bowls with scallions, salted roasted peanuts and lime. The paste gave the whole thing an aromatic depth that would have required considerably more shopping and chopping to achieve from scratch.

Pacific Foods chicken miso ramen broth: The foundation of one of my favorite recent semi-homemade dinners. I like to doctor it with a little additional miso and coconut cream for richness, then pile on noodles, protein, vegetables and toppings.

Brown or mushroom gravy packets: Listen. I know how to make gravy. I also know that sometimes a packet of gravy is exactly what a weeknight cottage pie or a skillet full of meatballs needs. There is absolutely no shame in that.

Frozen ginger, onion and garlic cubes: Perhaps the least glamorous but most indispensable items on this list. They eliminate chopping, cut down on dishes and make the first few minutes of cooking almost frictionless. Iâm happy to buy whichever brand happens to be available or on sale.

Of course, a grocery list is only so useful without a little inspiration. Here are five dinners that show how these ingredients make their way onto my table.

These arenât formal recipes. Think of them as invitations to improvise.

This one is a little more ambitious, but itâs an excellent example of how convenience ingredients can leave more room for creativity.

I started with Pacific Foods chicken miso ramen broth, adding extra miso and coconut cream for richness, then used chicken Iâd already grilled earlier in the week for protein.

While the broth heated, I tossed frozen mushrooms, ginger and onions with oil, soy sauce and red pepper flakes, then roasted everything until the edges were almost charred. I steamed frozen corn and edamame, and tossed a generous pile of shredded red cabbage with sesame oil.

Into the bowls went noodles, broth, chicken, vegetables and roasted toppings, along with soy sauce eggs Iâd marinated earlier that day. I served a salad with homemade carrot-ginger dressing alongside.

Not exactly a five-minute dinner, but a beautiful one. And because so much of the prep was already done, I could spend my time on the little details that made the meal feel special.

This is the dinner for when I want something cozy and substantial but do not want to peel a single potato.

Brown ground beef or chicken in a skillet with frozen onions, garlic and mushrooms. Once everything has developed some color, stir in a brown or mushroom gravy packet, a splash of stock and a generous quantity of frozen mixed vegetables.

Let the filling simmer until thick and savory, then transfer it to a baking dish (or keep it in an oven-safe skillet, if you have one). Spread deli-counter mashed potatoes over the top and bake until the filling is bubbling and the potatoes are golden in spots.

Hearty, comforting and full of vegetables, without having to peel, chop or mash a thing.

This is one of those dinners that started with a can and became something much more interesting.

I browned a little hot Italian sausage in a skillet, then added sun-dried tomatoes, a can of tomatoes, Heydayâs tomato alla vodka beans, a splash of cream and frozen spinach.

Everything simmered together into a rich, savory, slightly spicy skillet situation. I served it with toasted sourdough tips for scooping up all that lovely sauce.

The beans bring both flavor and fiber, the sausage adds richness and heat, and the spinach practically disappears into the sauce. I would happily eat this again tomorrow.

This is the sort of thing I love making when I want something fresh, bright and satisfying without spending much time at the stove.

Cook some small pasta â Iâm fond of cubetti here â and add frozen peas and carrots, cooking them just long enough to heat through. Drain, cool slightly and toss with canned white beans and a generous amount of Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto.

You can eat it slightly warm or chill it for later. Either way, the creamy, lemony pesto ties everything together, while the vegetables and beans make the whole thing more substantial.

Sometimes you just need one very good sauce.

Remember those Whole Foods chicken cutlets I was raving about earlier? Hereâs one of my favorite things to do with them.

While the cutlets cook, toast some soft potato buns and make a quick lemon-garlic mayonnaise. I use Kewpie, into which I stir freshly grated lemon zest and one of those handy frozen minced-garlic cubes, thawed.

When the chicken is nearly done, melt a slice of Muenster cheese over each piece.

To assemble, spread sun-dried tomato pesto on one half of the bun and the lemon-garlic mayo on the other. Add the cheesy chicken cutlet, then pile on an almost unreasonable quantity of fresh arugula. My beloved shredded cabbage would also be wonderful here if youâre in the mood for extra crunch.

The result is creamy, tangy, savory, crunchy and a little peppery. Itâs the sort of sandwich Iâd happily pay a cute restaurant a slightly unreasonable amount of money to make for me.

Instead, Iâm standing in my own kitchen, feeling very pleased with myself.

#6021. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer’s first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

New York City Democratic Socialists hold a rally in Union Square on Nov. 16, 2025, to mark the start of a campaign to tax the rich and win universal childcare. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu)

PARENTS SHOULDN’T NEED THE HELP OF CONGRESS TO SEE THEIR CHILDREN’S SCHOOL CURRICULUM

The New York initiatives are part of a larger effort by the DSA to incorporate childcare and political education into its organizing activities.

The organization's efforts to introduce socialist ideas to children date back at least a decade.

Items on a table during an election night party held by the Democratic Socialists of America-LA chapter at The Greyhound on Nov. 4, 2025 in Los Angeles, Calif. (Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

She warned that the impact could become more visible as newly elected DSA-backed officials take office.

"We're gonna see a lot more of the firsthand resources and the effects of this brand new class of DSA members being folded into their communities," Marré said.
